structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
The excerpt is a table of contents for Swedbank’s 2024 Sustainability Report, structured around ESRS and EU Taxonomy requirements. It covers:
- Basis for preparation: how the sustainability statement is compiled and any specific circumstances affecting reporting.
- Strategy and business model: description of strategy, business model and value chain; stakeholder interests and views; and material impacts, risks and opportunities (IRO) and their interaction with strategy.
- Managing IRO: processes to identify and assess material IROs and cross-references to ESRS disclosure requirements covered.
- Governance: the roles of the Board and CEO in sustainability, information they receive and topics addressed, incentive schemes, due diligence statement, risk management and internal controls, and Swedbank governance documents.
- Environmental information: reporting aligned with the EU Taxonomy, climate change disclosures (ESRS E1), and taxonomy-aligned tables.
- Social information: own workforce (ESRS S1) and consumers/end-users (ESRS S4).
- Governance information: business conduct (ESRS G1) and financial crime.

structure.title: General disclosures
structure.heading: General disclosures
structure.start_phrase: Swedbank’s sustainability report has been prepared in accordance with the Swedish Annual Accounts Act for Credit Institutions and Securities Companies (ÅRKL) and the Swedish Annual Accounts Act (ÅRL),
structure.summary:
- Purpose and scope: General disclosures on the basis for preparing Swedbank’s sustainability statement, aligned with new EU sustainability reporting rules and presented at Group consolidation level consistent with the financial statements.
- Reporting framework: Voluntary early application of CSRD via ESRS (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772), inclusion of mandatory EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures, and adherence to ÅRKL/ÅRL as amended by CSRD. First formal application in Sweden is for financial years starting after June 2024, but Swedbank applies it for this report.
- Subsidiary reporting: Estonian, Latvian, and Lithuanian subsidiaries are subject to national CSRD-aligned rules but are exempt from separate sustainability reports because the Group report covers them (Directive 2013/34/EU Article 19a.9).
- Value chain boundary: Upstream (capital acquisition, purchasing), downstream (customer engagement and financial services), and supporting functions (compliance, KYC, HR, IT). For 2024, coverage is limited to first-tier direct customers and suppliers. Detailed description is in ESRS 2 SBM-1.
- Intellectual property: No omissions of information related to IP rights, know-how, or innovation results.
- Sustainability risk information: Additional risk disclosures are provided under CRR (EU) 575/2013 in the Risk and Capital Adequacy Report on Swedbank’s website.
- Changes in presentation: Transition from GRI and TCFD indices to CSRD/ESRS; prior indices are omitted. Significant design, scope, and disclosure-level changes reduce comparability with prior years. Any corrections, amendments, or recalculations are explained within relevant sections.
- Time horizons and estimates: Time horizons defined per disclosure and described in IRO 1. Use of estimates and external data is explained per metric (e.g., financed emissions), with data quality indicators. Swedbank plans to improve data availability, internal controls, and IT systems to reduce reliance on estimates.
- Action plans: Presented within each thematic ESRS standard; actions are embedded in core products and services. No significant incremental operating or capital expenditures identified, and no dependencies on external preconditions (e.g., subsidies or policy changes).
- Phase-in choices for 2024: Use of ESRS phase-ins for:
  - ESRS 2 SBM-3 paragraph 48(e) (anticipated financial effects)
  - ESRS E1-9 (anticipated financial effects from material climate-related physical and transition risks and potential opportunities)
  - ESRS S1-7 (non-employee worker characteristics), S1-11 (social protection), S1-12 (persons with disabilities), and S1-14 paragraphs 88d–88e (non-employee reporting and work-related ill health metrics).

nodes.title: Basis for preparation
nodes.heading: BP Basis for preparation
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank’s sustainability report has been prepared in accordance with the Swedish Annual Accounts Act for Credit Institutions and Securities Companies (ÅRKL) and the Swedish Annual Accounts Act (ÅRL),
nodes.summary:
This section explains how Swedbank’s 2024 sustainability report is prepared and scoped. It is compiled at Group level on the same consolidation basis as the financial statements and, although Swedish CSRD-based rules formally apply from financial years starting after June 2024, Swedbank has voluntarily adopted CSRD and ESRS (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772) this year, including Article 8 EU Taxonomy disclosures. The report aligns with Swedish Annual Accounts Acts (ÅRKL/ÅRL) as amended by CSRD. Subsidiaries in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are individually in scope of local CSRD rules due to their size and public-interest status, but are exempt from separate sustainability reports because the Group report covers them (Article 19a.9).

The value chain is defined into upstream (capital acquisition, purchasing) and downstream (customer engagement, delivery of financial services), supported by compliance, KYC, HR and IT; for 2024, the scope is limited to first-tier customers and suppliers. No information on intellectual property, know-how or innovation has been omitted. Additional sustainability risk information required under CRR (Regulation (EU) 575/2013) is provided in the Risk and Capital Adequacy Report on the website.

Due to the CSRD transition, GRI and TCFD indices are omitted, disclosure design and scope have materially changed, and comparability with prior years is limited; any corrections or recalculations are explained within relevant sections. Time horizons used for disclosures are defined in the IRO-1 methodology; the report explains where estimates and external data are used (e.g., financed emissions) and indicates data quality, with plans to improve data availability, internal controls and IT to reduce estimation, especially for monetary amounts.

Action plans are presented within each ESRS thematic standard and are embedded in business operations and offerings; no significant standalone operating or capital expenditures or specific external preconditions have been identified. Swedbank is phasing in certain ESRS disclosures for 2024, including: ESRS 2 SBM-3 paragraph 48(e) (anticipated financial effects), ESRS E1-9 (anticipated financial effects from climate risks and opportunities), and ESRS S1 items S1-7, S1-11, S1-12, and parts of S1-14 related to non-employee reporting and work-related ill-health metrics.

nodes.title: Preparation of the sustainability statement
nodes.heading: Preparation of the sustainability statement, BP-1
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank’s sustainability report has been prepared in accordance with the Swedish Annual Accounts Act for Credit Institutions and Securities Companies (ÅRKL) and the Swedish Annual Accounts Act (ÅRL),
nodes.summary:
- Basis of preparation and framework: Swedbank’s sustainability report is prepared at Group level on the same consolidation basis as the financial statements, in line with the Swedish Annual Accounts Acts (ÅRKL/ÅRL) as amended by the EU CSRD (Directive 2022/2464). Although not yet mandatory (first FY beginning after June 2024), Swedbank applies CSRD voluntarily for 2024, preparing disclosures under ESRS (Commission Delegated Regulation 2023/2772) and including EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures.
- Subsidiary reporting: CSRD-aligned rules are in force in Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania. Swedbank’s Baltic subsidiaries (public-interest entities with >500 employees) are exempt from individual sustainability reports because the Group report covers them (Article 19a(9) of Directive 2013/34/EU).
- Value chain scope: The value chain is defined as upstream (e.g., capital acquisition, purchasing) and downstream (customer engagement and delivery of financial services), supported by functions such as compliance, KYC, HR, and IT. For 2024, coverage is limited to first-tier direct customers and direct suppliers.
- Intellectual property: No information on IP rights, know-how, or innovation results has been omitted.
- Sustainability risk disclosures: Additional sustainability risk information is provided under CRR (Regulation EU 575/2013) in the Risk and Capital Adequacy Report on Swedbank’s website.
- Changes vs prior years: GRI and TCFD indices are omitted due to CSRD/ESRS equivalence. The report’s design, scope, and disclosure level have changed significantly under CSRD, creating comparability challenges with prior years. Any corrections, amendments, or recalculations are explained within relevant sections.
- Time horizons and estimates: Time horizons are defined per disclosure (referenced to IRO-1). Use of estimates and external data is explained at metric level, with data quality indicated (e.g., financed emissions). Data quality is expected to improve as more companies publish data and through enhanced internal controls and IT; Swedbank will collect newly mandatory data to reduce reliance on estimates.
- Action plans: Presented within each thematic standard, focused on integrating sustainability into products and services as part of daily operations. No significant incremental operating or capital expenditures identified; actions are not contingent on external preconditions (e.g., subsidies or policy shifts).
- ESRS phase-in choices for 2024: 
  - ESRS 2 SBM-3 paragraph 48(e): anticipated financial effects (phased in)
  - ESRS E1-9: anticipated financial effects from material physical and transition risks and potential climate-related opportunities (phased in)
  - ESRS S1-7: characteristics of non-employee workers (phased in)
  - ESRS S1-11: social protection (phased in)
  - ESRS S1-12: persons with disabilities (phased in)
  - ESRS S1-14: reporting on non-employees and work-related ill health/days lost (paragraphs 88d–88e) (phased in)

nodes.title: Specific circumstances
nodes.heading: Specific circumstances, BP-2
nodes.start_phrase: As reporting under the CSRD includes equivalent information as previously reported in accordance with the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) and Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD), these indices have been omitted from this year’s report.
nodes.summary:
- Reporting basis and scope: Swedbank’s Group sustainability report is voluntarily prepared in line with CSRD and ESRS (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772), and includes EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures. It follows the same consolidation as the financial statements under Swedish ÅRKL/ÅRL. Baltic subsidiaries (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania) are individually in scope of local CSRD rules but exempt from separate reports due to Group-level reporting (Article 19a.9).

- Value chain boundary: The value chain is defined as upstream (capital acquisition, purchasing) and downstream (customer engagement, financial services), with supporting functions (compliance, KYC, HR, IT). For 2024, reporting is limited to first-tier direct customers and suppliers.

- Intellectual property: No omissions of information related to IP, know‑how, or innovation results.

- Sustainability risks: Additional risk information is disclosed under CRR (EU 575/2013) in the Risk and Capital Adequacy Report.

- Changes vs prior years: Transition from GRI and TCFD indices to CSRD/ESRS; indices are omitted. The new framework materially changes design, scope and disclosure depth, limiting comparability with prior reports. Corrections/recalculations are explained within relevant sections.

- Time horizons and estimates: Time horizons are defined per disclosure (see IRO-1). Estimates and external data are used for several metrics (e.g., financed emissions) with data quality indicated; Swedbank plans to improve data quality via better internal controls/IT and expanded data collection to reduce estimation uncertainty.

- Action plans and funding: Action plans are provided within each thematic ESRS; sustainability actions are embedded in business-as-usual operations with no significant incremental capex/opex identified and no reliance on external preconditions.

- ESRS phase-ins applied (2024): Deferred disclosures include ESRS 2 SBM-3 48(e) (anticipated financial effects), ESRS E1-9 (anticipated financial effects from climate risks/opportunities), and ESRS S1 items (S1-7 non-employee worker characteristics; S1-11 social protection; S1-12 persons with disabilities; S1-14 elements on non-employees and work-related ill health).

- Strategy and integration: Sustainability is core to strategy and aligned with the vision of a financially sound and sustainable society across environmental, social, financial and ethical dimensions. The bank supports customer transition through sustainable products, financing, incentives, and advisory; maintains sectoral positions (e.g., climate, nature, arms/defense); and engages publicly to influence industry and policy.

- Operational footprint and procurement: As a digital bank with physical touchpoints, Swedbank works to reduce IT/data center energy use and emissions, and leverages procurement to impose robust sustainability requirements on a large supplier base.

- Climate impact and lending: Emissions are both direct and predominantly indirect via customers. Targets are aligned with the Paris Agreement. Lending spans mortgages and corporate sectors (notably real estate, agriculture/forestry, manufacturing, retail/wholesale). About 80% of lending is real estate-related; the bank finances property and infrastructure and provides sustainability expertise to accelerate sector transition. Energy efficiency is a priority amid rising electrification.

- People and culture: Swedbank aims to be an inclusive, engaging workplace with supportive initiatives; total headcount at year-end was 19,217 across Sweden and international locations.

- Business conduct and ethics: The Code of Conduct guides decisions beyond legal compliance, with mandatory onboarding and annual ethics training for all employees.

- Financial crime prevention: Strong KYC, due diligence, and transaction monitoring to combat fraud, money laundering, and terrorist financing; executive-level commitment to robust, effective controls to protect customers, shareholders, and society.

structure.title: Strategy
structure.heading: SBM Strategy
structure.start_phrase: As a bank that performs a vital societal function, Swedbank has an important role to play in the transition to a sustainable society.
structure.summary:
- Swedbank positions sustainability at the core of its strategy, aligned with the vision of a financially sound and sustainable society across environmental, social, financial and ethical dimensions.
- The bank commits to supporting customers’ transition through sustainability-oriented financing and investments, minimizing climate impact and energy use, promoting equality, diversity and inclusion, and combating financial crime.
- Sustainability is integrated into operations via products, services and financial incentives; selective customer engagement is guided by positions on climate, nature, and arms/defense, and the bank participates in public discourse to influence broader transition.
- As a digital bank with physical touchpoints, Swedbank works to reduce energy use and emissions from data centers and IT infrastructure, and leverages procurement to enforce strict sustainability standards on suppliers.
- Climate impact management includes Paris-aligned targets to reduce both direct and especially indirect (financed) emissions; lending choices can contribute to or detract from climate goals, with opportunities in renewable energy, transport electrification and sustainable agriculture.
- Roughly 80% of lending is tied to the real estate sector; Swedbank offers mortgages, property loans and advisory, and provides sustainability expertise to drive transition in a high energy-consuming sector where energy efficiency is critical amid growing electrification.
- The bank aims to meet society’s substantial investment needs while pursuing its own climate targets, recognizing the income potential of sustainable financing and advisory.
- People and culture: Swedbank seeks to be an attractive, inclusive employer that develops and engages employees; the workforce totaled 19,217 in 2024, primarily in Sweden and the Baltics.
- Business conduct is anchored in a Code of Conduct that goes beyond legal compliance to ethical decision-making, reinforced through onboarding and annual ethics training for all employees.
- Combating financial crime is a top priority, with robust customer due diligence, continuous monitoring and governance oversight to protect the bank’s services from misuse and uphold obligations to customers, shareholders and society.

nodes.title: Strategy, business model and value chain
nodes.heading: Strategy, business model and value chain, SBM-1
nodes.start_phrase: As a bank that performs a vital societal function, Swedbank has an important role to play in the transition to a sustainable society.
nodes.summary:
- Swedbank embeds sustainability at the core of its strategy, aligning with a vision of a financially sound and environmentally, socially, financially and ethically sustainable society.
- The bank supports customers’ sustainability transitions through dedicated products, services and financial incentives, while being selective in corporate engagements guided by positions on climate, nature, and arms/defense; it also engages in public debate to influence broader transition.
- Operational integration includes reducing digital footprint (data centers and IT), and leveraging procurement with strict supplier sustainability requirements.
- Climate strategy targets significant reductions in direct and indirect greenhouse gas emissions in line with the Paris Agreement, acknowledging that most impact is indirect via lending to customers.
- Lending portfolio exposures span real estate, agriculture/forestry, manufacturing, and retail/wholesale; financing renewables, transport electrification and sustainable agriculture can lower emissions and create revenue, while carbon‑intensive financing raises indirect emissions.
- Real estate is the dominant exposure (about 80% of lending); Swedbank provides mortgages, property loans and advice, supports housing, commercial property and infrastructure, and contributes sustainability expertise to accelerate the sector’s transition; energy efficiency is a key focus amid rising electrification.
- People and culture: Swedbank aims for an inclusive, engaging workplace with supportive initiatives; total employees were 19,217 in 2024 (down from 19,341 in 2023), mainly in Sweden and the Baltics, with smaller presences in other Nordic countries, the USA, China and Spain.
- Business conduct is governed by a comprehensive Code of Conduct emphasizing ethical decisions beyond legal compliance, reinforced through onboarding and annual ethics training.
- Strong focus on combating financial crime: preventing fraud, money laundering and terrorist financing through due diligence and continuous monitoring; the Executive Committee prioritizes robust defenses to protect systems, products and services, fulfilling regulatory, systemic and moral responsibilities.

nodes.title: Business model and key elements of the value chain
nodes.heading: Business model and key elements of the value chain
nodes.start_phrase: With 7.4 million private customers and 553 000 corporate customers, Swedbank is one of the leading banks in its four home markets: Sweden, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
nodes.summary:
- Swedbank is a leading bank in Sweden, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania, serving 7.4 million private and 553,000 corporate customers.
- Operates through four Business Areas: Swedish Banking; a new Premium & Private Banking area (created in 2024); Corporates & Institutions (now includes corporates formerly served in Swedish Banking); and Baltic Banking. Despite these changes, the 2024 strategy and business model remain unchanged.
- Value chain structure:
  - Upstream: capital acquisition via customer deposits and capital markets, liquidity management, and procurement to ensure stability, efficiency, and competitiveness.
  - Own operations (supporting functions): compliance, KYC, employee engagement, risk assessment, and IT infrastructure.
  - Downstream: customer/relationship management and distribution through branches and digital channels; offerings include deposits, lending, insurance, payments, investment advice, and asset management.
- Stakeholder integration: continuous customer dialogue across Business Areas informs strategy; partnerships expand sustainability expertise (e.g., improving property energy performance) and support development of sustainable products and services.
- Performance monitoring: regular assessment of the sustainability profile of investment and lending portfolios; tracking of internal impacts such as climate footprint and employee engagement.
- Strategic focus: sustainable value creation to enhance customer profitability and long-term stability; maintaining secure, reliable digital and operational infrastructure; robust risk management to balance risk and return, uphold trust among customers, investors, and regulators, and ensure systemic stability.
- Stakeholders across the value chain: upstream investors and suppliers; internal employees and the Board; downstream private and corporate customers, society, and the broader operating environment.
- Key product/service usage areas: Financing; Savings & Investments; Payments & Cards; Trading & Capital Markets.
- Additional details on strategy and business model are provided elsewhere in the report (pages 10–23).

nodes.title: Sustainability-related targets
nodes.heading: Sustainability-related targets
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank Group has adopted sustainability-related targets in several different areas.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and approach: Swedbank sets sustainability targets across lending, asset management, and its own operations, developed through ongoing dialogue with employees, investors, and customers. Targets apply across all geographies and cover both private and corporate customers, with a strong focus on reducing indirect (financed) emissions.
- Overarching climate objective: Achieve net‑zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 and align lending and investment portfolios with the 1.5‑degree pathway, supported by interim targets.
- Own operations: Reduce operational emissions by 60% by 2030 versus 2019.
- Lending portfolio sector targets (covering 79% of total lending; target year 2030 vs 2019 baseline):
  - Mortgages: −39% financed emission intensity (kgCO2e/m2).
  - Commercial properties: −43% financed emission intensity (kgCO2e/m2).
  - Oil and gas (exploration, production, refining): −50% absolute financed emissions (tCO2e).
  - Power generation: −59% financed emission intensity (tCO2e/MWh).
  - Steel: −29% financed emission intensity (tCO2e/t steel).
  - Shipping: 0% alignment delta by 2030 versus the IMO’s most ambitious reduction trajectory (i.e., fully aligned).
- Asset management (Swedbank Robur):
  - Alignment: 1.5‑degree alignment by 2025; net‑zero by 2040.
  - Reduced emissions: Halve Robur’s emissions by 2030; increase the share of AUM invested in companies with science‑based/net‑zero targets to 60% by 2030 and 100% by 2040.
  - Climate solutions: Raise the share of AUM in renewable energy to 1.4% by 2030 and 3.8% by 2040.
  - Engagement: Conduct dialogues with companies in material sectors covering 70% of financed emissions, expanding to more sectors over time.
- Sustainable financing ambitions (by 2027):
  - At least triple sustainable lending volume versus 2022.
  - Ensure ESG bonds represent at least 40% of issues where Swedbank acts as advisor.
- Granularity note: While climate targets are linked to industries, there is not yet a specific, detailed assessment at the individual product, service, or market level; the sustainable financing ambition is framed in general terms.
- People and culture targets: Increase employee engagement measured via an engagement index and sustainable employee index (covering workplace attractiveness, learning and development, work‑life balance). Equality and diversity targets include KPIs to monitor pay gaps and achieve balanced gender distribution among managers.
- References: Additional details are available in Targets E1‑4 and S1‑5; links to material impacts, risks, and opportunities are mapped on pages 82–84.

nodes.title: Sustainable products and services
nodes.heading: Sustainable products and services
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank’s starting point is that the transition to a sustainable society must take place in close collaboration with customers.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on customer collaboration to enable the transition to a sustainable society, emphasizing ongoing dialogue to understand clients’ transition plans and tailor products, services, and advice.
- Ambition to at least triple sustainable lending by 2027 versus 2022, with sustainable lending defined as the Sustainable Asset Registry plus sustainability-linked loans (utilised credit and granted but not utilised commitments).
- 2024 progress: total sustainable lending volume reached SEK 187bn; reported gross carrying amount of SEK 151bn equals 8.37% of total customer loans (SEK 1,806bn). Growth driven by +SEK 54bn in the Sustainable Asset Registry and +SEK 21bn in sustainability-linked loans/commitments.
- Product offering:
  - Private customers: loans for solar panels and energy efficiency, green mortgages with rate discounts for high energy-class properties, and car loans/leasing with environmental criteria.
  - Corporate customers: ESG-related bonds (green, social, sustainability-linked), green loans, green equities, sustainability-linked loans, and sustainability advice.
- EU Taxonomy alignment: assets primarily in energy-efficient properties and sustainable corporate activities under NFRD/CSRD; alignment disclosed by turnover and CapEx across operating segments, with 2024 segment reporting updated to separate Premium & Private Banking and restated comparatives.
- Sustainable Funding Framework enables issuance of green and social bonds; eligible categories define inclusion in the Sustainable Asset Registry; annual impact reporting via the Sustainable Bond Impact Report.
- Sustainable Asset Registry expanded to SEK 128bn (from SEK 74bn), comprising SEK 119bn in green and SEK 9bn in social categories. Growth led by green buildings (mortgages, commercial real estate, tenant-owner associations) and renewable energy (notably in the Baltics), supported by improved energy performance data and advisory partnerships (Hemma for Swedish retail, Ramboll for Swedish property corporates). Continuous product and advisory development highlighted as key to further scaling sustainable financing.

nodes.title: Sustainability-linked loans
nodes.heading: Sustainability-linked loans
nodes.start_phrase: Sustainability-linked loans are offered to larger companies and institutions that want to improve their sustainability work.
nodes.summary:
- Sustainability-linked loans (SLLs): Offered to larger companies/institutions to incentivize improved sustainability performance. Interest rates are tied to meeting predefined sustainability KPIs; loans can be used for general corporate purposes. Performance is tracked via regular reporting. If aligned with the EU Taxonomy, loans are included in Swedbank’s EU Taxonomy reporting.

- 2024 SLL developments: Volume rose 55%, including utilized credit and granted but not utilized commitments. Growth was led by the industrial segment, followed by property. Common KPIs are Scope 1 and 2 emissions (absolute and intensity); Scope 3 is increasingly used as data quality improves.

- Sustainable lending volumes (SEKm, 2024): 
  - Sustainable Asset Registry (SAR) – green categories: 119,345 (notably green buildings, renewable energy, clean transportation, pollution prevention, natural resources, water/wastewater, energy efficiency).
  - SAR – social categories: 8,813 (socioeconomic advancement and empowerment, employment generation, affordable housing).
  - Total SAR: 128,158.
  - Sustainability-linked loans: 23,043.
  - Total sustainable lending: 151,201.
  - SLLs granted but not utilized commitments: 36,271.
  - Combined sustainable lending plus unutilized SLL commitments: 187,472.
  - Note: 2024 introduces Premium and Private Banking as a separate segment; comparative figures restated. 2023 figures adjusted for identified errors in Baltic Banking social category assets.

- Green and social bonds: Swedbank has SEK 76.55bn outstanding.
  - 2024: Five green bonds issued in EUR/SEK totaling SEK 27.36bn; proceeds allocated to green categories in the SAR.
  - Social bonds: First Nordic bank to issue in 2023; proceeds directed to SAR social categories (e.g., SME lending in socioeconomically challenged areas, lending to female-owned businesses).
  - Outstanding by year (SEKm): Green bonds 70,808 (2024), 40,982 (2023), 27,872 (2022); Social bonds 5,743 (2024), 5,555 (2023).

- Sustainability analysis in the lending process: Swedbank integrates sustainability risk into credit decisions.
  - Scope: Corporate customers with annual turnover > SEK 500m (> EUR 50m Baltics) and/or assets > SEK 1,000m (> EUR 100m Baltics) where credit exposure ≥ SEK 8m (≥ EUR 0.8m Baltics); also applied to others with exposure/limit ≥ SEK 8m.
  - Method: New digital tool used across all Business Areas; assesses sector-specific ESG risks to identify material issues, producing sustainability ratings for both sector and customer.
  - Risk management: Customers categorized into low/medium/high sustainability risk; high-risk cases escalated to the Group risk function for guidance alongside credit decisions.
  - Support: Sector guidelines and position statements provide industry insights, key questions, and focus areas.

nodes.title: Savings and investments
nodes.heading: Savings and investments
nodes.start_phrase: Responsible and sustainable investments have become an important factor in generating long-term returns, and the Group has a long tradition of conveying knowledge about money and savings.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on responsible savings and investments, emphasizing the role of financial literacy, personalized advice, and the importance of emergency buffers, insurance, and long-term saving.
- Asset management integrates sustainability and aligns with EU SFDR and EU Taxonomy to improve transparency and enable sustainable choices.
  - Swedbank Robur is the primary asset manager, largest by AUM in Sweden and the Baltics (market shares: Sweden 22%; Estonia 40%; Latvia 39%; Lithuania 37%).
  - Product strategy: simple, sustainable, innovative; 5 Article 9 funds; majority of fund AUM in Article 8; most discretionary mandates are Article 8.
  - Taxonomy-aligned AUM (SEKbn): turnover-based 33 (2024) vs 20 (2023); CapEx-based 52 (2024) vs 31 (2023).
  - AUM including life insurance (SEKbn, 2024 vs 2023): Article 9 funds 12 vs 2; Article 8 funds 1,831 vs 1,512; Article 6 funds 110 vs 101; total fund AUM 1,953 vs 1,614; discretionary/closed funds 481 vs 428; total AUM 2,433 vs 2,042.
- Insurance offerings via Swedbank Insurance cover pension, capital, personal, and risk insurance for private and corporate customers, guided by a Sustainability Policy across investment types.
  - All unit-linked products offered are SFDR Article 8; traditional insurance not classified; variable universal life not classified due to broad investment options.
  - Life insurance Taxonomy-aligned AUM as of 31 Dec 2024: SEK 4,665m (turnover-based) and SEK 6,097m (CapEx-based).
  - In the Baltics, P&C and Life Insurance subsidiaries (under Swedbank Estonia) offer property, motor, travel, payment protection, life insurance, and investment products; these products are Article 8 with enhanced sustainability controls.
- Business ethics and position statements:
  - Commitment to legal compliance and ethical standards; group-wide positions on climate/nature and arms/defence.
  - Defence sector services only when aligned with UN, EU, or US sanctions; no services to entities linked to controversial or nuclear weapons; applies to financing, investment decisions for financial products, and capital market services.
  - No new financing/capital market financing for companies extracting oil, gas, thermal coal, or thermal peat (limited exceptions for qualifying transition cases with Paris-aligned plans).
  - No direct financing of coal/peat power generation or companies earning >5% from these; no direct financing of new oil/gas power stations, new oil tankers, or new oil refineries.
  - Investment exclusions (where Swedbank makes decisions) for companies with >5% income from extraction or power generation from oil, gas, thermal coal, or thermal peat; certain transition exceptions possible; indirect third-party funds and client discretionary decisions are excluded from this policy.
- Payments and cards: broad range of secure, customer-centric payment services, with strong internal controls and collaborations to prevent criminal misuse.
- Trading and capital markets: active arranger of ESG bonds with a target of ≥40% ESG share by 2027; in 2024, ESG bonds were 36% of arranged transactions.
  - 2024 ESG activity: 117 transactions; SEK 61bn arranged volume; share of total arranged volume 36%; cumulative since start SEK 267bn.
- Stakeholder engagement: continuous dialogue with four main groups—customers, employees, owners/investors, and society—plus a wide range of other stakeholders including regulators, NGOs, academia, suppliers, savings banks, and ratings agencies.

nodes.title: Interests and views of stakeholders
nodes.heading: Interests and views of stakeholders, SBM-2
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank maintains an ongoing dialogue with various stakeholders and has grouped these into four main stakeholder groups:
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on responsible, sustainable savings and investments as drivers of long-term returns, coupled with Swedbank’s role in boosting financial literacy through tailored advice, promoting savings buffers and insurance.

- Asset management:
  - Sustainability integrated throughout; alignment with EU SFDR and EU Taxonomy to improve transparency and enable informed customer choices.
  - Swedbank Robur manages most assets; leading market shares (Sweden 22%; Baltics 37–40%).
  - Product strategy centers on simple, sustainable, innovative offerings; 5 Article 9 funds; majority of fund assets and most discretionary mandates classified as Article 8.
  - Growth in taxonomy-aligned assets (2024: SEK 33bn turnover-based; SEK 52bn CapEx-based).
  - Total assets under management rose to SEK 2,433bn (fund AUM SEK 1,953bn; Article 8 funds SEK 1,831bn; Article 9 funds SEK 12bn).

- Insurance:
  - Swedbank Insurance offers pension, capital, personal and risk insurance; sustainability policy covers investments in traditional, unit-linked and variable universal life.
  - All unit-linked policies offered are Article 8; traditional and variable universal life not classified under SFDR.
  - Life insurance taxonomy-aligned AUM (2024): SEK 4.7bn turnover-based; SEK 6.1bn CapEx-based.
  - In the Baltics, P&C and Life Insurance subsidiaries classify products as Article 8 with enhanced sustainability oversight.

- Business ethics and position statements:
  - Commitment to legal compliance and ethical standards with group-wide positions on climate/nature and arms/defense.
  - No financing or capital market services for extraction of oil, gas, thermal coal or thermal peat (limited exceptions for transition plans); restrictions on coal/peat power and new oil/gas infrastructure.
  - Exclusions in Swedbank-led investments for companies deriving >5% revenue from fossil extraction or power (transition exceptions under strict criteria); indirect third-party funds not covered.
  - No services to entities involved with controversial or nuclear weapons.

- Payments and cards:
  - Broad, secure payment and card services with strong internal controls to prevent criminal misuse.

- Trading and capital markets:
  - Active arranger of ESG bonds; 2024: 117 transactions, SEK 61bn, representing 36% of arranged volume; ambition for ESG bonds to be ≥40% by 2027; cumulative arranged ESG volume SEK 267bn.

- Stakeholder engagement:
  - Four primary groups: customers, employees, owners/investors, society; additional stakeholders include regulators, NGOs, academia, suppliers, etc.
  - Customer engagement via digital channels, branches, events; continuous surveys, structured complaints process, customer ombudsmen.
  - Employee engagement through continuous surveys, development reviews, board representation, and a European Works Council.
  - Ongoing dialogue with owners/investors/analysts through reports, meetings, and disclosures.
  - Collaboration with regulators and industry bodies in Sweden and the EU to shape effective sustainability regulation; media monitoring and participation in sustainability initiatives.

- Double materiality assessment (2024):
  - Built on 2023 stakeholder surveys/interviews and expanded with internal workshops; affected communities not included.
  - Stakeholders prioritize climate transition and sustainable products; employees emphasize social engagement and employer attractiveness.
  - Annual strategy review reinforced climate direction, focusing on financing the energy transition in the real estate sector.

- Human rights, DEI, and data protection:
  - Human Rights Policy aligned with international frameworks (UDHR, EU Charter, ECHR, ILO, UNCRC, UNGPs); application across all markets and relationships.
  - DEI policy ensures equal opportunities and zero tolerance for discrimination, harassment, and bullying; ongoing evaluation and dialogue.
  - Strong data protection commitments via GDPR compliance and banking confidentiality to safeguard personal data and privacy.

nodes.title: Interests and views of stakeholders
nodes.heading: Interests and views of stakeholders, S1 SBM-2
nodes.start_phrase: Respect for human rights is a fundamental element of Swedbank’s operations, strategy and business model.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on stakeholder dialogues as a core part of Swedbank’s sustainability and strategy work, covering customers, employees, owners/investors/analysts, and society/regulators.
- Customer dialogues: Primarily digital with support from branches/events; sustainability-focused communications; continuous feedback integration via surveys; structured five-step complaints process with responsible case handling and customer ombudsmen; aim to raise satisfaction and competitiveness.
- Employee dialogues: Continuous digital surveys to track well-being, engagement, risks and opportunities; promote open feedback culture; results managed within units; development reviews with line managers; HR reports insights to Executive Committee; employee representation on the Board and via the European Works Council.
- Owners, investors, analysts: Ongoing engagement through reports, meetings, calls, website, and press releases; feedback informs bank development; profitability and returns viewed as contributing to societal benefit.
- Society and regulators: Active collaboration with national and EU authorities and industry bodies (e.g., Swedish Bankers’ Association, ESBG, EBF) to shape effective sustainability-related regulation; dialogue outcomes feed into regulatory implementation and compliance; media monitoring informs improvements; participation in sustainability initiatives.
- Double materiality assessment: 2024 assessment built on 2023 stakeholder surveys/interviews and expanded with internal workshops; stakeholders included investors, customers, suppliers, employees, unions, academia, NGOs (not affected communities); key themes—climate transition, sustainable products/services, social engagement, employer attractiveness; annual strategy review integrates these views, reinforcing climate-related strategic choices, especially financing the energy transition in real estate.
- Human rights and DEI (S1 SBM-2): Human Rights Policy aligned with international frameworks (UDHR, EU Charter, ECHR, ILO, UNCRC, UNGPs); commitment across all markets and relationships; DEI policy ensuring equal opportunities and zero tolerance for discrimination, harassment, and bullying, with continuous follow-up.
- Data protection and privacy (S4 SBM-2): Central to operations via Code of Conduct; GDPR compliance ensuring transparency and individual rights; protection reinforced by Swedish banking secrecy; aim to uphold legal duties and human rights to data protection.

nodes.title: Interests and views of stakeholders
nodes.heading: Interests and views of stakeholders, S4 SBM-2
nodes.start_phrase: Respect for human rights is central to Swedbank’s operations, strategy and business model.
nodes.summary:
- Customer dialogues: Swedbank engages customers mainly through digital channels, branches, events, seminars on sustainability, and media/marketing. Feedback is continuously integrated via private and corporate customer surveys, a five-step complaints process (with responsible case handling and feedback to customers), and customer ombudsmen. Purpose: drive high customer satisfaction and long-term competitiveness.

- Employee dialogues: Priorities highlighted include a good work environment, work-life balance, and skills development. Continuous digital surveys track employee sentiment, impacts, risks, and opportunities, and help drive behavior change and open feedback cultures. Results are discussed within units, complemented by development reviews with managers. Group HR & Facility Management reports insights to the Group Executive Committee. Employees are represented on the Board (with deputies) and through a Group-wide European Works Council.

- Owners, investors, and analysts: Ongoing dialogue via quarterly reports, the Annual and Sustainability Report, meetings (virtual/physical), calls, website updates, and press releases. Feedback informs business development. Strong profitability and returns are positioned as benefiting society through investments and social engagement.

- Society and regulators: Continuous engagement with authorities and policymakers in sustainability-related matters, both directly and via industry bodies. Memberships include the Swedish Bankers’ Association (Sustainability Council/Committee), ESBG (Sustainable Finance/CSR Committees), EBF, European Energy Efficiency Financing Coalition, ESG Financial Markets Task Force, and IIF Sustainable Finance Policy Expert Group. Dialogues primarily with Swedish agencies (e.g., Ministry of Finance, FSA) and EU institutions (European Commission, ECB, EBA). Aim: contribute expertise to effective regulation that enables banks’ role in a more sustainable society; outcomes inform implementation and compliance. The bank monitors sustainability-related media and participates in sustainability initiatives.

- Stakeholder dialogue in the double materiality assessment: 2024 assessment built on 2023 stakeholder surveys/interviews (investors, customers, suppliers, employees, unions, academia, NGOs) and expanded with internal workshops; affected communities were not included. Key feedback: customers prioritized climate transition and sustainable products/services; employees emphasized social engagement and attractiveness as an employer. External/internal analyses underpin strategy. The annual strategy review incorporated stakeholder views and reinforced climate-related strategic choices, especially financing the energy transition in the real estate sector.

- Human rights, DEI, and data protection (Interests and views of stakeholders, S1 SBM-2 and S4 SBM-2): Swedbank’s Human Rights Policy aligns with international frameworks (UDHR, EU Charter, ECHR, ILO Declaration, UNCRC, UNGPs) and applies across all markets and business relationships, promoting respect for human rights and a sustainable financial system. The Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Policy commits to equal opportunities, zero tolerance for discrimination/harassment/bullying, and ongoing evaluation. Data protection is governed by the Code of Conduct and GDPR compliance, ensuring transparency, individual rights, and banking confidentiality to protect customer privacy.

nodes.title: Material impacts, risks and opportunities and their interaction with strategy and business model
nodes.heading: Material impacts, risks and opportunities and their interaction with strategy and business model, SBM-3
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank’s material impacts, risks and opportunities identified in the materiality assessment for the year are presented below.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Presents Swedbank’s material impacts, risks and opportunities (IRO) across environmental, social and governance topics, how they manifest across the value chain (upstream, own operations, downstream), expected time horizons, related disclosure requirements, whether targets exist, and brief descriptions of each IRO.

- Value chain framing: Defines downstream (e.g., lending, asset management), own operations (Group Functions and direct operations), and upstream (purchasing). Identifies where material IROs concentrate and within what timeframes they may occur.

- Environmental (E1 Climate change and Energy):
  - Adaptation: Potential negative downstream impact if lending supports businesses not adapted to climate change; opportunity in growing demand for green financing and advisory.
  - Mitigation: Potential positive downstream impact by financing renewables/electrification; actual negative impact upstream/downstream/own operations via exposure to high emitters; transition risk of credit losses if policy/technology/market shifts; opportunity in green products and climate advice.
  - Energy: Actual negative downstream impact from financing fossil-intensive energy consumption; transition risks tied to emissions and energy-efficiency policies; opportunities in energy-transition enablers, efficiency loans and green mortgages.
  - References to ESRS E1 disclosures (E1-1–E1-4, E1-6) and targets elsewhere.

- Social:
  - S1 Own workforce: Working conditions (potential positive via good conditions and inclusive culture; potential negative via stress/unsocial hours, inadequate wages/freedom of association); opportunities to attract/retain talent; risks from uncompetitive conditions and potential legal exposure on equal pay; equal treatment and opportunities for all (potential negative if deficient; opportunity through gender balance, reduced pay gaps, training, harassment prevention); other work-related rights (privacy/data handling risks). Primarily short-to-medium term, in own operations. Targets referenced to S1-5.
  - S4 Consumers and end-users: Information-related impacts from handling large volumes of sensitive data; potential negative effects on individuals and society from breaches; financial risk from deficiencies in IT and information handling. Short term, own operations and downstream.

- Governance:
  - G1 Business conduct: Corporate culture (potential negative if governance/controls/transparency are weak; regulatory and brand risk); whistleblower protection (potential negative impact on trust and rights if mismanaged); supplier relationships and payment practices (potential negative upstream impacts and financial/brand risk if poorly managed); corruption and bribery (exposure in customer-facing and procurement roles; legal, brand and financial risks if controls inadequate). Time horizons range short to long term across value chain segments.
  - Entity-specific: Combatting financial crime: Potential negative impacts on society, employees, stakeholders and financial stability if AML/CFT/fraud controls are inadequate; short-term financial and reputational risks from deficiencies. Downstream and own operations.

- Strategic integration and gaps:
  - Materiality assessment informs Group-wide strategy strengthening, but no formalized process yet to evaluate how material IROs affect strategy, business model, value chain and decision-making, nor linkage of impacts to strategy/model.
  - No Group-wide evaluation of current short-term financial impacts from material IROs; climate strategy resilience assessed via scenarios and stress tests, but without a Group-wide qualitative/quantitative analysis; additional details referenced in E1 SBM-3.

- Materiality assessment approach (IRO-1):
  - 2024 update extends the 2023 double materiality assessment to meet ESRS and EFRAG guidance, with deeper value chain mapping across Sweden, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
  - Method: Four steps—(1) business context and value chain mapping, (2) identification of IROs across lending, asset management and own operations plus stakeholder input, (3) assessment of impact and financial materiality using ESRS criteria and Swedbank’s ESG risk framework, (4) determination of reporting scope.
  - Stakeholder engagement: External (investors, customers, suppliers, NGOs, researchers) and internal (employees, unions, subject experts) via surveys/interviews/workshops; supported by sector sources (e.g., SASB) and due diligence.
  - Assessment criteria: For financial materiality—likelihood and financial effect of risks/opportunities; for impact materiality—scale, scope, irremediability, and likelihood (for potential impacts).

- Year-over-year continuity and changes:
  - Material areas largely consistent with the prior year; biodiversity differs in 2024.
  - Topic designations updated to align with ESRS sub-topics, so labels may differ from the previous year.

- Targeting and cross-references: Notes where measurable, time-bound targets exist and points to related sections (e.g., Strategy, business model and value chain SBM-1; E1-4; S1-5).

structure.title: Managing impacts, risks and opportunities
structure.heading: IRO Managing impacts, risks and opportunities
structure.start_phrase: Prior to the report for the financial year 2023, a double materiality assessment was conducted at a general level.
structure.summary:
- Scope and gaps: Swedbank integrates materiality assessment results into group-wide strategic work but lacks a formalized process to evaluate how material impacts, risks, and opportunities affect strategy, business model, value chain, and decision-making, or how these impacts link to the Group’s strategy and model.
- 2024 assessments: No evaluation was conducted of short-term financial impacts from material risks and opportunities on the Group’s financial position, results, and cash flow. Climate strategy resilience was tested via scenarios and stress tests, but no Group-wide qualitative or quantitative analysis was performed (further details referenced in E1 SBM-3).
- Materiality outcomes: This year’s results align with the prior year’s material areas, except for biodiversity; topic designations differ due to alignment with ESRS sub-topics (further details in IRO-1).
- Double materiality approach: The 2024 assessment was expanded to meet ESRS/EFRAG guidance, focusing on deeper value chain mapping and identifying impacts, risks, and opportunities across the chain, considering both impact materiality (effects on people and environment) and financial materiality (financial effects from sustainability factors).
- Methodology (four stages): 
  1) Analyze business context and map the value chain; 
  2) Identify impacts, risks, and opportunities across operations and the value chain with stakeholder input; 
  3) Assess and determine impact and financial materiality using ESRS-recommended criteria and Swedbank’s ESG risk framework; 
  4) Define the reporting scope based on results.
- Value chain focus: Covers home markets (Sweden, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania). Most material issues arise downstream via customers (e.g., lending); upstream (purchasing, capital acquisition) and own operations (e.g., employer responsibilities) are also evaluated. Operations analyzed via three units: Lending, Asset management, Own operations.
- Stakeholder engagement: Multi-method dialogue (questionnaires, interviews, workshops) with external stakeholders in 2023 (investors, customers, suppliers, researchers, NGOs) and expanded in 2024 to internal stakeholders (employees, unions, experts), including both affected stakeholders and users of disclosures.
- Topic identification sources: NGO reports, industry surveys and indices (e.g., SASB), academic research, and significant business activities (lending portfolio, investments). A comprehensive topic list was built from ESRS-defined topics and stakeholder insights and assessed uniformly.
- Assessment criteria: 
  - Material impacts: actual and potential, positive and negative, evaluated by scale, scope, irremediability (plus likelihood for potential impacts), informed by stakeholder dialogue and due diligence. 
  - Financial materiality: risks and opportunities evaluated by likelihood and financial effect.

nodes.title: Process to identify and assess material sustainability topics
nodes.heading: Process to identify and assess material sustainability topics, IRO-1
nodes.start_phrase: Prior to the report for the financial year 2023, a double materiality assessment was conducted at a general level.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and intent: Swedbank integrates results of its double materiality assessment into Group-wide strategic work to identify gaps not covered by the current strategy, aiming to strengthen it. However, a formalised process to evaluate how material impacts, risks and opportunities affect the strategy, business model, value chain and decision-making—and whether impacts are linked to the strategy and business model—has not yet been developed.

- 2024 evaluations and resilience: For 2024, Swedbank did not evaluate the current short-term financial impacts of material risks and opportunities on the Group’s financial position, results and cash flow. Climate strategy resilience has been explored via scenario analyses and stress tests, but no Group-wide qualitative or quantitative analysis has been conducted. References are provided to Strategy and business model (E1 SBM-3) and Managing impacts, risks and opportunities (IRO-1).

- Continuity and change in material topics: The 2024 materiality assessment aligns with the prior year’s material areas, with biodiversity as the notable change. Because 2024 followed ESRS sub-topic definitions, topic designations differ from the prior year.

- Alignment with ESRS/EFRAG: A general double materiality assessment was conducted prior to FY 2023; in 2024 it was extended to meet ESRS 1 and EFRAG guidance, with a stronger focus on mapping the value chain and identifying impacts, risks and opportunities throughout it.

- Methodology (four stages):
  1) Analysis of business context and mapping of the value chain.
  2) Identification of impacts, risks and opportunities across own operations and the value chain, informed by stakeholder input.
  3) Assessment and determination of impact materiality and financial materiality using ESRS-recommended criteria and Swedbank’s ESG risk framework.
  4) Determination of reporting scope based on results.

- Value chain scope and focus: The mapping covers all home markets (Sweden, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania). As a financial institution, the most relevant sustainability issues are downstream (e.g., customers via lending), with upstream factors (procurement, capital acquisition) and own operations (e.g., employer responsibilities) also assessed.

- Analytical units: The assessment divides operations into Lending, Asset management, and Own operations.

- Stakeholder engagement: 
  - 2023: External stakeholders (investors, customers, suppliers, researchers, NGOs) engaged via surveys, interviews, and workshops.
  - 2024: Expanded to internal stakeholders (employees, unions, subject matter experts), covering both affected stakeholders and users of disclosures.

- Topic identification sources: Stakeholder insights; ESRS-defined sustainability topics; NGO reports; industry surveys and indices (e.g., SASB); relevant research; and significant business activities (loan portfolio, investments). A comprehensive “gross list” of topics was created and assessed consistently.

- Assessment criteria:
  - Impact materiality: Evaluates positive/negative actual and potential impacts using scale, scope, irremediability, and likelihood.
  - Financial materiality: Evaluates risks and opportunities using likelihood and financial effect.
  - Assessment informed by stakeholder dialogue and existing due diligence processes.

- Reporting outcome: The scope of sustainability reporting is set based on the double materiality results, with detailed methodology and outcomes referenced in IRO-1.

nodes.title: Methodology
nodes.heading: Methodology
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank has developed a method for double materiality assessment in accordance with ESRS 1 and EFRAG’s guidance.
nodes.summary:
- Swedbank incorporates double materiality assessment results into Group strategy but lacks a formal, Group-wide process to evaluate how material impacts, risks, and opportunities affect strategy, business model, value chain, and decision-making.
- For 2024, no Group-wide evaluation was conducted of short-term financial impacts from material risks and opportunities on financial position, results, or cash flow. Climate strategy resilience was explored via scenario analyses and stress tests, but without a comprehensive Group-wide qualitative or quantitative assessment (referenced in E1 SBM-3).
- The 2024 materiality outcomes largely mirror the prior year, except for biodiversity; topic designations changed due to alignment with ESRS sub-topics (further detail in IRO-1).
- The double materiality assessment was expanded in 2024 to meet ESRS and EFRAG guidance, emphasizing deeper value chain mapping and identification of impacts, risks, and opportunities across Swedbank’s operations and value chain.
- Methodology follows four stages: (1) analyze business context and map the value chain; (2) identify impacts, risks, and opportunities using stakeholder input; (3) assess impact and financial materiality per ESRS criteria and Swedbank’s ESG risk framework; (4) set reporting scope based on results.
- Value chain mapping covers Sweden, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania. Material issues are primarily downstream via customers (e.g., lending), with relevant upstream considerations (procurement, capital acquisition) and own operations (as employer). Analysis units: lending, asset management, and own operations.
- Stakeholder engagement included external stakeholders in 2023 (investors, customers, suppliers, NGOs, researchers) and expanded to internal stakeholders in 2024 (employees, unions, experts) through questionnaires, interviews, and workshops; both affected stakeholders and disclosure users were included.
- Topic identification drew on stakeholder insights, ESRS-defined topics, and sector sources (NGO reports, industry surveys/indices like SASB, research), creating a comprehensive topic list assessed uniformly.
- Assessment criteria: material impact considers positive/negative actual and potential impacts using scale, scope, and irremediability (plus likelihood for potential); financial materiality evaluates risks and opportunities by likelihood and financial effect. Existing due diligence processes and stakeholder dialogue informed the assessment.

nodes.title: Assessment of impact materiality and financial materiality
nodes.heading: Assessment of impact materiality and financial materiality
nodes.start_phrase: In 2024, internal stakeholders, such as subject matter experts and representatives from different Business Areas, were consulted in the work to assess impacts, risks and opportunities in different sustainability areas.
nodes.summary:
- In 2024, Swedbank ran cross-functional workshops with internal stakeholders to identify material sustainability topics across the value chain, applying Group risk time horizons: short (1–3 years), medium (3–10 years), long (10+ years).
- Impact materiality used four dimensions: scale (1–4), scope (1–4), irremediability (time to restore from easy to irreversible), and likelihood (1–4). Scoring averaged scale, scope, and irremediability and, where applicable, multiplied by likelihood. Both actual (from due diligence) and potential impacts (where data is limited) were assessed; likelihood was applied to potential impacts. No prioritization or monitoring of impacts occurred in 2024.
- Financial materiality evaluated financial impact (1–4) and likelihood (1–4), with the outcome as impact × likelihood and equal weighting of parameters. The impact assessment informed financial materiality. Climate risk methods are most advanced; other sustainability risks and opportunities are primarily assessed qualitatively. Examples considered included risks from real estate lending and opportunities in energy efficiency financing.
- ESG risk management: annual risk-based planning prioritizes ESG risks via top-down and bottom-up views over short- and long-term horizons, supporting strategy, risk appetite, and feeding ICAAP stress testing. There is not yet an explicit process to integrate identified impacts into the established risk management process.
- Validation and governance: materiality assessments used four-point scales aligned to Swedbank’s ESG risk framework. Results were compiled, validated with participants, and the final list of material topics was decided by the Head of Brand, Communication and Sustainability, then presented to the CEO, Group Executive Committee, and Board.
- Reporting scope: material topics were mapped to specific disclosure requirements and data points for the 2024 report, with ownership assigned to relevant experts. Work began to establish internal controls for sustainability reporting, including the double materiality assessment (referenced in GOV-5).

nodes.title: Swedbank’s material topics in the value chain
nodes.heading: Swedbank’s material topics in the value chain
nodes.start_phrase: An overview of the outcome of Swedbank’s double materiality assessment 2024 is illustrated below.
nodes.summary:
- Presents Swedbank’s 2024 double materiality assessment and maps where topics arise across the value chain (upstream, own operations, downstream), distinguishing impact materiality from financial materiality (risks/opportunities).
- Material topics identified:
  - Environment: climate change mitigation across the value chain; climate change adaptation and energy considered within the assessment.
  - Social: own workforce (working conditions; equal treatment and opportunities; other work-related rights); consumers and end-users (information-related impacts).
  - Corporate governance: business conduct (supplier relationship management including payment practices, corporate culture, anti-corruption and bribery, whistleblower protection); combating financial crime.
- Topics assessed as not material in 2024 under ESRS: pollution, water and marine resources, biodiversity, and circular economy, due to low portfolio exposure to high-impact sectors and operating contexts with strong environmental regulation; affected communities were not included and no consultations were held in 2024.
- Change from 2023: biodiversity was material in 2023 (driven by external stakeholder input) but not in 2024 after an updated methodology incorporating internal stakeholders, portfolio analysis, and alignment with TNFD and EFRAG showed limited lending exposure to biodiversity-impactive sectors.
- Biodiversity assessment approach and limitations: qualitative analysis using available data, TNFD guidance, and an internal pilot for exposure analysis; challenges include limited sector-specific science-based guidance, lack of universally quantifiable metrics, and insufficient quality-assured customer data, leading to a focus on potential rather than actual impacts; commitment to further methodological development and future reassessment.
- Nature-related risk assessment methods: use of NGFS scenarios for physical and transition risks in sector analyses; evaluation of sector dependencies on ecosystem services; geospatial impact/dependency analysis of financed properties in key biotopes, nature reserves, and Natura 2000 areas; criteria informed by the WWF Biodiversity Risk Filter and TNFD.

nodes.title: Areas that were not deemed to be material
nodes.heading: Areas that were not deemed to be material
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank’s materiality assessment is based on the company’s exposure to the thematic sustainability topics defined in the ESRS.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Presents Swedbank’s 2024 double materiality assessment, mapping where sustainability topics are material across the value chain (upstream, own operations, downstream) as impact and/or financial materiality (risks/opportunities).

- Material topics across the value chain:
  - Environment: Climate change mitigation (across the chain) and adaptation; energy in own operations.
  - Social: Own workforce (working conditions; equal treatment and opportunities; other work-related rights); consumers and end-users (information-related impacts).
  - Governance: Business conduct (whistleblower protection; supplier relationship and payment practices; corporate culture; anti-corruption and bribery) and combating financial crime.

- Non-material topics in 2024 and rationale:
  - Pollution; water and marine resources; biodiversity; circular economy not deemed material due to low exposure to affected sectors and operating in countries with strong environmental legislation.
  - Affected communities were not included as a stakeholder group; no consultations with affected communities in 2024.

- Change from 2023:
  - Biodiversity was material in 2023 (driven by extensive external stakeholder dialogue).
  - In 2024, methodology was updated to place greater weight on internal stakeholders and portfolio analysis aligned with TNFD and EFRAG guidance; limited lending exposure to biodiversity-impacting industries led to biodiversity not being material.

- Biodiversity/nature-related assessment approach and limits:
  - Conducted a qualitative analysis using TNFD guidance, an internal pilot on exposure tools, WWF Biodiversity Risk Filter criteria, and NGFS scenarios.
  - Included sector-level dependency/impact assessment and geospatial screening of financed properties in key biotopes, nature reserves, and Natura 2000 areas.
  - Challenges: immature practices in banking, limited science-based sector guidelines, lack of universally quantifiable metrics and quality-assured customer data; focus on potential rather than actual impacts. Swedbank could not assess whether it operates in areas with sensitive biodiversity. NGFS scenarios do not capture systemic ecosystem collapse.
  - Commitment to continue developing methodology and revisit materiality as data and methods improve.

- Climate topic (E1 IRO-1) process and methods:
  - Analysis units: lending (financed emissions); asset management (Swedbank Robur Fonder); own operations (Scope 1–3 and climate-relevant procurement).
  - Impact identification:
    - Lending: Measures financed emissions with focus on emission-intensive sectors; 2030 sector targets aligned with a 1.5°C pathway; participation in NZBA and assessment of its ten emission-intensive sectors to enable customer data collection and target monitoring.
    - Asset management: Uses SFDR’s Principal Adverse Impact (PAI) indicators to assess climate impacts of investments.
    - Own operations: Reviews Scope 1–3 emissions; assesses supplier geography due to energy mix and infrastructure differences.
  - Risk identification (physical and transition):
    - Applies EBA’s three-method toolkit: risk framework (scenario analysis, stress testing), exposure method (counterparty-level ESG risk), and portfolio alignment.
    - Scenario analysis: Uses NGFS “Net Zero 2050” (~+1.4°C), “Delayed transition” (~+1.7°C), and “Current policies” (~+3.0°C) with macro variables (GDP, inflation, carbon price) and physical risk hazards (floods, heatwaves, droughts); augments property lending with geodata; expert assessment of expected credit losses and operating losses; ICAAP includes a 10‑year resilience scenario.
    - Stress testing: Three-year scenario-driven tests integrating physical and transition risks within ICAAP.
    - Exposure-level ESG tool: SASB/IFRS-based industry materiality mapping, customer questionnaire on ESG management, resulting in ESG scores and classification (high/medium/low ESG risk).

- Financial reporting note:
  - 2024 climate scenarios did not affect financial statements; climate risks are expected to materialize primarily via credit risks/credit losses; effects not yet sufficiently quantifiable for expected credit loss overlays.

nodes.title: Process to identify and assess material sustainability topics
nodes.heading: Process to identify and assess material sustainability topics, E1 IRO-1
nodes.start_phrase: The process to identify and assess material sustainability topics in the area of climate was divided into three analysis units.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and limitations of scenarios: NGFS scenarios used; they exclude systemic ecosystem collapse but include higher average temperatures and more frequent extreme weather, especially considered for agriculture and forestry. Swedbank has not assessed whether it operates in biodiversity-sensitive areas.

- Materiality process (E1 IRO-1): Assessment covers Lending, Asset Management (Swedbank Robur Fonder), and Own Operations, with separate views on impacts, risks, and opportunities. Climate scenarios did not affect 2024 financial statements; climate risks are expected to materialize mainly via credit risk/credit losses. Additional expected credit losses tied to climate scenarios are not yet quantifiable/material.

- Methods to identify and assess climate impacts:
  - Lending: Measures financed emissions, prioritizing emission-intensive sectors; 2030 sector targets aligned with a 1.5°C pathway; membership in NZBA; sector focus enables customer data collection and target tracking.
  - Asset management: Uses SFDR Principle Adverse Impact (PAI) indicators to assess actual/potential climate impacts of investments.
  - Own operations: Reviews Scope 1–3 emissions and climate-relevant procurement sectors; evaluates supplier geography due to regional energy/infrastructure differences.

- Methods to identify and assess climate-related risks (physical and transition):
  - Framework: Recognizes uncertainty, long-term nature of risks, and early-stage methodologies linking climate to credit risk. Applies EBA’s three methods: risk framework (incl. scenario analysis, stress testing), exposure method (counterparty ESG risk), and portfolio alignment (loan book alignment with climate goals).
  - Scenario analysis (risk framework): Uses NGFS Net-Zero 2050 (1.4°C), Delayed Transition (1.7°C), and Current Policies (3.0°C) with macro and physical risk drivers; supplements property lending analysis with geodata; expert assessment of impacts on expected credit losses and operating losses. ICAAP includes a 10-year resilience scenario.
  - Stress tests: Three-year ICAAP stress tests integrate physical and transition risks.
  - Exposure methodology: ESG analysis tool based on SASB/IFRS materiality; generates industry- and customer-specific ESG scores and high/medium/low ESG risk classifications.
  - Portfolio alignment: Measures financed emissions and sets 1.5°C-aligned credit portfolio targets to both support customer transition and manage climate risk exposure.
  - Physical risk assessment: For real estate, applies SMHI methodology and IPCC RCP 8.5; identifies properties sensitive to climate events by geography and scenario.
    - Sweden: 4% of real estate–collateralized loans show heightened physical risk (3% acute risk).
    - Baltics: 1% of residential property–collateralized loans show heightened physical risk; sea-level rise not assessed.

- Time horizons and maturities:
  - Definitions: Short term 1–3 years; medium term 4–10 years; long term >10 years. NGFS scenarios extend to 2050; Delayed Transition emphasizes 2030; Current Policies emphasizes late-period physical risks.
  - ICAAP: 10-year horizon to 2034; short-term 3-year analysis of a stressed transition on profitability/capital.
  - Lending terms and exposures:
    - Transition risk: ~SEK 554bn to companies/tenant-owner associations with heightened transition risk; 70% property-related; property average remaining term 9 years; most other sectors 0–3 years (electricity production ~4 years).
    - Physical risk: Residential loans ~SEK 1,037bn; heightened-risk subset (~4%) average term just over 22 years. Commercial property loans in Sweden ~SEK 154bn; heightened-risk subset average term 10 years.
    - Implication: Long terms in property lending necessitate long-term scenarios; shorter terms elsewhere allow proactive exposure adjustment. Strategy emphasizes transitioning with customers toward net zero by 2050.

- Geographic/materiality conclusions:
  - Own assets and supply chain: Physical climate risks deemed non-material; no material climate risks identified in the supply chain.
  - Lending: Transition risks assessed as material.

- Alignment and exclusions: Ongoing assessment of customers’ transition plans, emissions, and energy performance, including cash-flow sensitivity testing. Swedbank’s Position Statement on Climate Change and Nature lists sectors not financed/invested in as they are not 1.5°C-aligned.

- Asset management risk handling: Climate risks arise via underlying holdings and are assessed in each fund’s investment process; no standalone physical/transition risk analysis performed by Swedbank Robur Fonder, but company dialogues are conducted.

- Own operations risk management: Climate risks integrated into enterprise and operational risk frameworks via top-down and bottom-up identification and annual RCSA; procurement includes supplier climate risk and geography reviews. Physical risks to IT/office environments and supply chain remain non-material.

nodes.title: Risks identified in the short, medium and long term
nodes.heading: Risks identified in the short, medium and long term
nodes.start_phrase: A summary of the potential risks that were identified in the short, medium and long term is presented in the table below.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and framing: Swedbank summarizes climate-related risks and opportunities across short (1–3 years), medium (>3–10 years), and long term (>10 years) horizons, grounded in its ESG risk and double materiality assessments.

- Key climate-related risks
  - Short term: Credit risks from costly, uncertain electrification in energy/transport/materials; rising electricity prices due to higher demand and investment; refinancing risks for fossil‑dependent clients; lower demand for energy‑intensive buildings under new EU rules; reputational risk of greenwashing; business risk if client expectations for transition financing/advice aren’t met.
  - Medium term: Credit risks from higher emission allowance prices and capital‑intensive power sector investments driving electricity prices; widening valuation gaps between energy‑efficient and inefficient buildings; pressure on agricultural resilience from transition to sustainable practices; EU restoration rules weighing on protected forest land values and forestry profitability; growing legal dispute risk as sustainability liabilities strengthen; increased transition risk as circular models displace incumbents.
  - Long term: Systemic credit/market/liquidity risks from climate impacts on vulnerable economies and financial institutions (including within the EU), spilling into Swedbank’s home markets; stranded assets among lagging sectors and energy‑intensive buildings in weak‑demand locations; rising sea levels and more frequent flooding eroding property values and insurance cover; physical climate risks increasing financial strain and insurance erosion in agriculture and forestry.

- Methods to identify and assess transition opportunities
  - Lending: Business areas integrate sectoral transition analysis into planning, considering regulatory shifts, technology, and consumption trends; guided by the Swedbank Position Statement on Climate Change and Nature (updated annually) and double materiality work; examples include financing property energy efficiency.
  - Asset management: Swedbank Robur integrates climate opportunity assessments into fund/portfolio processes per its Engagement Strategy, with public annual reporting at fund level.
  - Own operations: No formal method yet; internal qualitative review indicates most opportunities arise downstream via customers and investments.

- Climate-related opportunities
  - Short term: Rising demand for property energy‑efficiency upgrades; growth in solar and wind in energy and property; increased need for transition advisory, sustainable products, and debt/capital issuance; partnerships to finance energy transition; financing of electrification, digitalization, and automation across sectors.
  - Medium term: Greater investment in climate adaptation for agriculture, forestry, and real estate; competitive edge from circular/resource‑efficient processes; deeper, insight‑driven lending to clients managing transition; broader demand for sustainability‑profiled products and services.
  - Long term: Longer growing seasons in Northern Europe boosting food and timber output; expanding bioeconomy creating new markets and segments through rising bioenergy demand.

nodes.title: Opportunities identified in the short, medium and long term
nodes.heading: Opportunities identified in the short, medium and long term
nodes.start_phrase: A summary of the opportunities that were identified in the short, medium and long term are presented in the table below.
nodes.summary:
- Defines short (1–3 years), medium (>3–10 years), and long (>10 years) horizons and summarizes climate‑related risks from Swedbank’s ESG risk and materiality assessment. Credit risk dominates across all horizons, driven by costly electrification, rising electricity prices, higher emission allowance prices, and technology uncertainty; sector‑specific risks include widening value gaps between energy‑efficient and inefficient buildings, refinancing challenges for fossil‑dependent customers, transition pressures in agriculture, and EU restoration rules affecting forest land values. Long‑term systemic risks include climate impacts on EU economies and financial institutions leading to credit, market, and liquidity risks, as well as stranded assets, rising sea levels and flooding eroding property values and insurance coverage, and physical climate risks in agriculture and forestry. Reputational greenwashing risk, strengthened legal liability, and business risk from failing to meet client transition expectations are also noted.

- Describes methods to identify and assess transition opportunities: in lending, sector analyses are integrated into business planning, guided by Swedbank’s annually updated Position Statement on Climate Change and Nature and a double materiality assessment; drivers include regulation, technology, and consumption shifts. In asset management (Swedbank Robur Fonder), opportunities are assessed within the investment process per the Engagement Strategy and reported annually by fund.
