For own operations and supply chain, no formal method exists yet; internal analysis indicates opportunities arise mainly downstream via customers and investments.

- Outlines opportunities by time horizon. Short term: growing demand for property energy efficiency, expansion of solar and wind, increased need for transition advisory and sustainable financing, partnerships to fund the energy transition, and financing of electrification/digitalization/automation. Medium term: higher adaptation investment in agriculture, forestry, and real estate; competitive advantages from circular and resource‑efficient processes; greater demand for sustainability‑profiled products and services; and expanded climate‑adaptation work with ag/forestry clients. Long term: longer Northern European growing seasons boosting food and timber output; a growing bioeconomy and bioenergy markets; and deeper lending to clients with strong transition strategies.

nodes.title: Process to identify material sustainability topics
nodes.heading: Process to identify material sustainability topics, G1 IRO-1
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank is systemically important in the financial system through its provision of financing solutions, investments and financial advice.
nodes.summary:
- Explains Swedbank’s process (G1 IRO-1) for identifying material sustainability topics, focusing on business conduct due to the bank’s systemic importance.
- Step 1: Business context analysis covering geography and customer groups, business and organizational structure, compliance framework and historical deficiencies, and ESG risk/materiality assessment; underscores the sector’s heavy regulation and the centrality of ethics and compliance to avoid sanctions and maintain credibility.
- Step 2: Identification and assessment of material impacts and financial materiality by internal experts with legal competence, integrating stakeholder views and aligning with existing processes that prioritize business conduct.
- Governance (GOV-11/G1 GOV-1): Defines roles of the Board (supervisory body) and CEO (administrative/management); the Board sets strategy and targets, ensures effective governance, risk management and compliance, adopts policies, and monitors external developments and conduct rules, grounded in internal/external regulations.
- Board composition and independence: No AGM-appointed members have operational roles; emphasis on diversity; gender parity (50/50); 9 of 10 members independent; inclusion of employee representatives and deputies; broad expertise across finance, real estate, macroeconomics, digitalization/AI, governance, ethics, law, and sustainability, with experience across Sweden and the Baltics.
- Board committees: Established to prepare matters without decision-making authority. The Remuneration and Sustainability Committee oversees sustainability strategy, business model, reporting, governance documents, monitors materiality assessment and identified opportunities/impacts, and ensures remuneration aligns with risk management and legal requirements.
- Sustainability governance structure: Outlines formal oversight and reporting lines among Shareholders/AGM, Board, President & CEO, business/product/group functions, External Auditors, Group Internal Audit, Board committees (Audit, Governance, Risk and Capital, Remuneration & Sustainability), and management forums (Group Asset Allocation, Group Risk & Compliance, Sustainable Bond Committee, ESG Reporting Forum, Sustainability Committee); notes Board appointment of the Deputy CEO, Head of Group Risk, and Head of Group Compliance.

structure.title: Role of the Board of Directors and the CEO
structure.heading: Role of the Board of Directors and the CEO, GOV-11
structure.start_phrase: The Board is the highest decision-making body after the AGM and the highest executive body.
structure.summary:
- Defines Swedbank’s governance for sustainability, clarifying the roles of the Board of Directors (supervisory body) and the CEO (administrative and management body).
- Board responsibilities: overall governance, strategy setting and follow-up, target setting, adoption of policies, oversight of risk management and compliance, and monitoring of the operating environment and conduct rules; none of the AGM-appointed Board members are operational.
- Board composition and independence: 10 AGM-appointed members (9 independent), gender balance 50/50; additional employee representatives and deputies from unions; diverse sectoral, functional, and regional expertise including banking, risk, governance, law, ethics, sustainability, and senior leadership backgrounds.
- Board committees and mandates:
  - Remuneration and Sustainability Committee: overall sustainability oversight (strategy, business model, reporting, governance), monitors materiality, opportunities and impacts; ensures remuneration aligns with effective risk management and legal requirements.
  - Audit Committee: ensures reliability and effectiveness of financial and sustainability reporting and related internal controls; oversees CEO’s procedures for risk management/internal control in reporting.
  - Governance Committee: evaluates the effectiveness and appropriateness of the governance model and processes.
  - Risk and Capital Committee: oversees identification, assessment, management, and reporting of risks in line with risk appetite, including sustainability-related risks; responsible for consumer/end-user risks (information security, cybersecurity, financial crime). All committees share responsibility for business conduct.
- Sustainability governance structure: outlines reporting lines among Shareholders/AGM, Board, CEO, Business Areas/Product Areas/Group Functions, and the role of External Auditors; notes Board appointment of the Deputy CEO, Head of Group Risk, and Head of Group Compliance.
- Board sustainability competence: assessed by the Nomination Committee and annual Board evaluation; targeted onboarding and ongoing training (Nasdaq Board programme, anti-corruption/ethics, CSRD focus in 2024); Group Sustainability regularly briefs the Board/RSC; Group Finance briefs the Audit Committee; Business Areas/Functions ensure competencies and training as regulations evolve.
- CEO and Group Executive Committee (GEC): 15 operational members, 47% women/53% men; rotating Chief Diversity Officer within GEC; CEO executes Board strategy, tracks sustainability KPIs (semi-annual to Board; quarterly to CEO from units), issues position statements on defense industry and climate change, and sets implementation instructions.
- CEO-established committees integrating sustainability:
  - Group Asset Allocation Committee: manages financial risks with sustainability factors considered across all risk types; chaired/decided by CFO; escalates as needed.
  - Group Risk and Compliance Committee: holistic oversight of non-financial risks and risk culture; sustainability embedded across risk types; chaired by Head of Group Risk; decisions by Head of Group Risk or Head of Group Compliance; escalates as needed.
  - Sustainability Committee: supports effective sustainability management/governance; chaired by Head of Group Brand, Communication & Sustainability; can escalate to CEO; open escalation path from all units.
  - ESG Reporting Forum: governs operational ESG reporting interpretations/definitions/assessments; chaired by Head of Group Finance.
  - Sustainable Bond Committee: decides on inclusion of green/social assets in the Sustainable Asset Registry; chaired by Head of Group Sustainability (veto right); majority-based decisions.
- Reporting and oversight: existing channels used to inform Board/CEO on impacts, risks, and opportunities; details on controls, integration with internal functions, targets, and progress appear in thematic chapters under “Metrics and targets” (including E1 Climate change and S1 Own workforce targets).
- Information flows to Board/CEO (GOV-2): regular updates on material impacts, risks, opportunities, stakeholder views from materiality assessment, due diligence processes, and the effectiveness of policies, measures, metrics, and targets; in 2024, quarterly reporting occurred to the CEO and GEC.

structure.title: Information provided to and sustainability matters addressed by the undertaking’s Board of Directors and CEO
structure.heading: Information provided to and sustainability matters addressed by the undertaking’s Board of Directors and CEO, GOV-2
structure.start_phrase: The Board and the CEO, including relevant committees, are regularly informed about material impacts, risks and opportunities by relevant units.
structure.summary:
- Governance structure and committee mandates:
  - Audit Committee: Oversees reliability and effectiveness of financial and sustainability reporting; ensures CEO maintains effective risk management and internal controls for these areas.
  - Governance Committee: Monitors and evaluates the effectiveness and appropriateness of Swedbank’s governance model and processes.
  - Risk and Capital Committee: Ensures procedures exist to identify, assess, manage and report risks, including sustainability-related risks identified via materiality assessment; responsible for risks affecting consumers/end users (information security, cybersecurity, financial crime).
  - Remuneration and Sustainability Committee: Overall responsibility for sustainability matters and employees.
  - All Board committees share responsibility for business conduct. Further details are in the Corporate Governance Report.

- Board sustainability competence and training:
  - Competence assessed by the Nomination Committee and through annual Board evaluations; a committee member has a special sustainability focus.
  - New directors receive induction on the Group, control functions, and governance framework; Nasdaq Board training provided.
  - Ongoing sustainability training coordinated by Group Sustainability; regular updates to the Board and committees (e.g., Audit Committee via Group Finance).
  - Recent focus areas: anti-corruption and bribery (in-depth training in 2022; ethics training incl. anti-corruption in 2024), current sustainability regulations (including CSRD). Business Areas and Group Functions ensure needed competencies as regulations evolve.

- CEO and Group Executive Committee (GEC):
  - GEC has 15 operational members; gender distribution 47% women, 53% men. Rotating Chief Diversity Officer function; during the year the CIO/Head of Group Channels and Technologies served in the role.
  - CEO executes Board strategy, with sustainability KPIs reported semi-annually to the Board; Business Areas/Product Areas/Group Functions report quarterly KPIs to the CEO.
  - CEO sets position statements on defense industry and climate change and issues instructions to implement policies.

- CEO-established committees integrating sustainability:
  - Group Asset Allocation Committee (chaired by CFO): Manages financial risks with sustainability considered across all risk types; can recommend escalation to Head of Group Risk, CEO, or Board.
  - Group Risk and Compliance Committee (chaired by Head of Group Risk): Holistic view of non-financial risks; embeds sustainability across risk types; decisions by Head of Group Risk or Head of Group Compliance; escalation to CEO/Board as needed.
  - Sustainability Committee (chaired by Head of Group Brand, Communication & Sustainability): Supports effective management/governance of sustainability; decisions by chair with escalation to CEO; open escalation channel from all Business Areas, Product Areas and Group Functions.
  - ESG Reporting Forum (chaired by Head of Group Finance): Governs operational ESG reporting issues, interpretations, definitions, and assessments.
  - Sustainable Bond Committee (chaired by Head of Group Sustainability with veto right): Decides on eligibility of loans as green/social assets for the Sustainable Asset Registry by majority vote.

- Reporting and oversight of impacts, risks, and opportunities (GOV-2):
  - Board and CEO receive regular information on material impacts, risks and opportunities, stakeholder views, due diligence implementation, and effectiveness of policies, measures, metrics and targets.
  - In 2024, quarterly reporting to the CEO, GEC and Board covered implementation of new sustainability reporting regulations.
  - Risk management processes for impacts/risks/opportunities described in IRO-1; Climate-related governance also reported under GOV-1; S1 Own workforce targets reported under S1-5.
  - Regular reporting on conflicts of interest and corruption; Corporate Governance Report lists topics discussed by the Board, CEO and GEC.
  - Material topics discussed in 2024 included climate change mitigation/adaptation, energy, working conditions, equal opportunities, employment rights, consumer information impacts, corporate culture, whistleblower protection, supplier relationship management and payment practices, corruption/bribery, and financial crime.

- Incentives and targets (GOV-3 and E1 GOV-3):
  - Board, CEO and GEC are excluded from Swedbank’s variable remuneration program; Board sets overarching sustainability targets aligned with strategy.
  - GEC is evaluated on sustainability metrics (e.g., employee engagement, net-zero by 2050, portfolio alignment with 1.5°C, increased sustainable financing) but without variable pay linkage.
  - Climate-related considerations are not factored into remuneration for Swedbank or for Swedbank Robur Fonder’s Board/management.

- Due diligence statement (GOV-4):
  - Due diligence is integrated throughout the Sustainability Report, covering:
    - Integration into governance, strategy and business model.
    - Stakeholder engagement across due diligence steps.
    - Identification and assessment of adverse impacts.
    - Actions to address adverse impacts.
    - Monitoring effectiveness and communicating outcomes.
  - Cross-references to ESRS disclosure requirements (ESRS 2, E1, S1, S4, G1) and relevant report sections/pages are provided.

- Additional notes:
  - Existing reporting channels to the Board/CEO are used for impacts/risks/opportunities; no dedicated GEC position for this.
  - Committee decision-making is generally by the chair with escalation paths; most committees are advisory except where specified.
  - Thematic chapters contain “Metrics and targets” sections detailing controls, procedures, targets and monitoring for each material topic.

structure.title: Incentive scheme
structure.heading: Incentive scheme, GOV-3
structure.start_phrase: Following a decision by the Annual General Meeting and the Board of Directors, Swedbank’s Board of Directors and the Group Executive Committee, including the CEO, are not entitled to participate in Swedbank’s variable remuneration incentive program.
structure.summary:
- Focus on governance of sustainability reporting at Swedbank, detailing how the Board of Directors and CEO oversee implementation of legal requirements and ESRS-aligned reporting.
- Explains information flows to the Board/CEO on material impacts, risks and opportunities, including results and effectiveness of policies, measures, metrics and targets, with cross-references to thematic chapters under “Metrics and targets,” S1 Own workforce (Targets S1-5), and E1 Climate change (GOV-1 Role of the Board and management).
- Describes how risk management is governed and overseen, with the Board/CEO’s role and processes referenced in IRO-1 (processes to identify and assess material impacts, risks and opportunities).
- Outlines due diligence governance and reporting via GOV-4, integrated into the Annual and Sustainability Report, and how the Board/CEO are informed through established reporting paths.
- Notes a 2024 reporting gap: no specific disclosure on how the Board/CEO (via the Group Executive Committee) considered trade-offs in decisions on major transactions and related risk management regarding impacts, risks and opportunities.
- Confirms regular Board/CEO reporting on conflicts of interest and corruption; Corporate Governance Report highlights topics discussed by the Board, CEO and GEC.
- Lists material sub-topics discussed in 2024: climate change adaptation and mitigation, energy, working conditions, equal treatment and opportunities, other employment law rights, information-related impacts for consumers/end-users, corporate culture, whistleblower protection, supplier relationship management (including payment procedures), corruption and bribery, and financial crime.
- Details incentive scheme (GOV-3): the Board, CEO and Group Executive Committee are excluded from variable remuneration programs; climate-related considerations are not factored into remuneration. The GEC is evaluated on sustainability metrics not linked to variable pay, aligned with objectives to increase employee engagement, achieve net-zero by 2050, align portfolios with the 1.5°C target, and increase sustainable financing.
- States equivalent remuneration stance for asset management (Swedbank Robur Fonder): Board, management and control function heads are excluded from variable remuneration; climate-related considerations are not included in pay.
- Provides a due diligence statement (GOV-4) mapping key due diligence elements to ESRS disclosure requirements: integrating due diligence into governance/strategy/business model (GOV-2, SBM-1, SBM-3); stakeholder collaboration across due diligence steps (GOV-2, SBM-1–2, IRO-1, E1-1, E1-4, SBM-3, S1-1–S1-4, G1-1–G1-3, G1-6); identifying/assessing adverse impacts (IRO-1, SBM-3); taking action to address impacts (MDR-A, E1-1–E1-4, SBM-3, S1-1–S1-5, S4-4, G1-1–G1-4, G1-6); and monitoring effectiveness and communication (MDR-T, MDR-M, E1-6, S1-3–S1-5, S4-5, G1-1–G1-4, G1-6), with page references to the Sustainability Report.

structure.title: Statement on due diligence
structure.heading: Statement on due diligence, GOV 4
structure.start_phrase: The reporting of Swedbank’s work on due diligence is integrated into the Sustainability Report and presented in the table below.
structure.summary:
- Describes Swedbank’s governance and reporting approach for sustainability, including how the Board of Directors, CEO, and Group Executive Committee oversee and are informed about material impacts, risks, opportunities, and the effectiveness of policies, measures, metrics, and targets.
- Points to where specific information is reported: “Metrics and targets” sections within each thematic chapter; S1 Own workforce (Targets S1-5); E1 Climate change (GOV-1); risk management processes and integration of impacts/risks/opportunities (IRO-1); due diligence governance and reporting pathway (GOV-4).
- Notes that in 2024 there is no specific reporting on how compromises related to impacts, risks, and opportunities were considered in major transaction decisions.
- Confirms regular reporting to the Board and CEO on conflicts of interest and corruption, with the Corporate Governance Report summarizing issues discussed by the Board, CEO, and Group Executive Committee.
- Lists material topics discussed in 2024: climate change adaptation and mitigation, energy, working conditions, equal treatment and opportunities, other employment rights, information-related impacts for consumers/end-users, corporate culture, whistleblower protection, supplier relationship management (including payments), corruption and bribery, and financial crime.
- Explains incentive scheme (GOV-3; E1 GOV-3): the Board, CEO, and Group Executive Committee are excluded from variable remuneration; climate-related considerations are not part of remuneration. The Group Executive Committee is evaluated (but not remunerated) on sustainability metrics tied to objectives such as employee engagement, net-zero by 2050, portfolio alignment with the 1.5°C goal, and increased sustainable financing.
- States that Swedbank Robur Fonder leadership is also excluded from variable remuneration and that climate factors are not considered in their remuneration.
- Provides an integrated due diligence statement (GOV-4), mapping key due diligence elements—governance integration, stakeholder engagement, impact identification/assessment, action, and effectiveness tracking/communication—to ESRS disclosure requirements (e.g., GOV-2, SBM-1/3, IRO-1, E1-1–E1-6, S1-1–S1-5, S4-4–S4-5, G1-1–G1-6), with page references where applicable.

structure.title: Risk management and internal controls
structure.heading: Risk management and internal controls, GOV-5
structure.start_phrase: The Board of Directors has overarching responsibility for ensuring that Swed-bank’s sustainability reporting is conducted in accordance with current legisla -tion.
structure.summary:
- Governance and oversight: The Board is accountable for compliant sustainability reporting. Group Finance (within the CFO Office) coordinates consolidation and ensures double materiality assessments align with CSRD, working closely with subject-matter experts across Group Functions. The double materiality method and outcomes were consulted internally and with external experts to meet regulatory requirements.

- Legislative implementation: Swedbank uses an established support and control process to identify and implement new or amended regulations; CSRD and EU Taxonomy have been managed through this process.

- Internal controls and ICFR integration: In 2024, Swedbank mapped sustainability reporting processes, identified highest-risk areas, and designed initial internal controls integrated with ICFR. The first wave focused on ESRS E1 (climate) and S1 (own workforce), with plans to expand to additional material ESRS standards in 2025.

- Key reporting risks and mitigations: Main risks are insufficient data quality, manual handling, and incorrect data consolidation. Mitigations include targeted control activities, data validation controls for uncertain data, duality controls for manual steps, and manager-led validations and reconciliations. System support to facilitate future reporting is being developed.

- EU Taxonomy controls: Controls were strengthened, applying definitions aligned with EBA reporting (e.g., property-collateralized loans). Reconciliations ensure consistency between EU Taxonomy, EBA reports, and Pillar 3 (including building energy classes). Ongoing reasonableness checks and sampling are performed.

- Continuous improvement and reporting: Internal control processes are continuously evaluated, with efforts to increase data availability via supplier requirements and engagement with external data providers. Implementation progress on sustainability reporting and internal controls will be reported regularly to the CEO and to the Board starting Q4 2024.

- Governance documents framework: Policies (Board-approved), instructions (CEO-approved), and directives (GEC-responsible owners) guide management of material impacts, risks, and opportunities. Regulatory framework owners are GEC members or designated security leaders unless otherwise decided. All governance documents undergo annual review and updates, considering external stakeholder input (e.g., AGM, dialogues, reports) and internal feedback to ensure regulatory alignment and organizational fit. Documents are available on the intranet; Group Legal issues update newsletters and distributes changes across the Group; public documents are on the website. “Upstream” and “downstream” terminology is generally not applied in individual documents and is not compiled for reporting.

- Examples of key governance documents:
  - Code of Conduct (public): Ethics framework guiding employee conduct, including data protection commitments.
  - Credit Policy (internal): Integrates ESG risks into credit assessments, transactions, and monitoring.
  - Customer Complaint Policy (internal): Governs handling of customer complaints and prevention of recurrences.
  - Environmental Policy (public): Sets the Group’s environmental approach, risk management, climate transition contribution, and operational energy reduction.
  - Human Rights Policy (public): Embeds respect for human rights in business decisions.

nodes.title: Swedbank’s governance documents
nodes.heading: Swedbank’s governance documents
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank’s governance documents describe processes and rules for handling issues relating to identified material impacts, risks or opportunities.
nodes.summary:
- Governance and accountability for sustainability reporting: The Board holds ultimate responsibility; Group Finance (CFO Office) coordinates consolidation and ensures the double materiality assessment complies with CSRD, working with subject-matter experts across Group Functions.
- Establishing sustainability reporting controls: In 2024 Swedbank began mapping processes, identifying high-risk areas, and designing initial internal controls under ICFR for ESRS E1 (climate) and S1 (own workforce), with expansion to additional ESRS standards planned in 2025.
- Key reporting risk areas and mitigations: Principal risks include data quality gaps, manual handling, and consolidation errors. Mitigations include targeted control activities, data validation for uncertain data, duality controls for manual steps, and manager-led control validations and reconciliations.
- EU Taxonomy internal control enhancements: Further developed controls include application of EBA-aligned definitions (e.g., property collateral), reconciliations between Taxonomy, EBA reporting, and Pillar 3 (e.g., building energy classes), ongoing reasonableness checks, and sampling.
- Systems and data improvements: Initiated system support for future reporting, enhanced data availability via supplier requirements and engagement with external data providers, and continuous evaluation of internal controls. Implementation progress reported regularly to the CEO and Board from Q4 2024.
- Double materiality methodology: Underwent multiple consultation rounds; internal experts provided inputs and external experts reviewed for regulatory compliance, transparency, and comparability.
- Governance framework overview: Comprehensive suite of policies, instructions, and directives defines processes and responsibilities for managing material impacts, risks, and opportunities. Regulatory framework owners (GEC members or designated security leaders) ensure implementation and follow-up.
- Governance document lifecycle: Annual review and updates incorporate external stakeholder feedback (e.g., AGM inputs) and internal viewpoints to ensure alignment with regulations and the governance model; public documents are published on Swedbank’s website; internal updates are communicated via Group Legal channels.
- Example governance topics: Code of Conduct; Credit Policy integrating ESG risk into credit processes; Environmental and Human Rights Policies; Enterprise Risk Management with ESG as a separate risk type; Diversity, Equity & Inclusion; Financial crime (AML/CTF, sanctions, anti-bribery, anti-fraud); whistleblowing; climate and controversial weapons position statements; work environment; procurement.
- External commitments and collaborations: Swedbank aligns with UN Global Compact, UNEP FI, UN Principles for Responsible Banking, the Net-Zero Banking Alliance, UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, and UN Women’s Empowerment Principles.
- EU Taxonomy scope and evolution: Describes criteria for alignment (substantial contribution, DNSH, minimum safeguards, technical screening). Reporting expanded over time—from eligibility (since 2021) to alignment for climate objectives (2023) and, in 2024, eligibility for the remaining four environmental objectives.
- Expanded KPI framework in 2024: Introduced a consolidated, segment-weighted KPI across banking, asset management, and insurance. Added detailed asset management and insurance tables. Fees/commissions and trading book will be added to the consolidated KPI in 2025. Non-financial activities are included but not Taxonomy-aligned.
- 2024 key metrics (stock and flow): 
  - Bank Green Asset Ratio (GAR) stock: 3.37% (turnover), 3.59% (capex); aligned assets SEK 64,290m (turnover) and SEK 68,504m (capex), driven by better data enabling more mortgage alignment and improved KPIs from NFRD/CSRD companies with all six environmental objectives.
  - GAR flow: 3.08% (turnover), 3.15% (capex); aligned flow SEK 8,412m (turnover) and SEK 8,646m (capex).
  - Asset management green ratio stock: 1.38% (turnover), 2.23% (capex); SEK 32,571m and SEK 52,450m, respectively. Denominator broadened to total AuM, lowering KPIs versus 2023 restated; increases reflect inclusion of financial institutions’ alignment and all six objectives.
  - Asset management flow (first year reported): 1.20% (turnover), 1.75% (capex); SEK 8,299m and SEK 12,126m.
  - Consolidated KPIs: 3.05% (turnover), 3.38% (capex). Gas and nuclear exposures mostly 0.00%, at most 0.70%.
- Data considerations: Data availability for Taxonomy alignment remains limited but is expected to improve and affect future KPIs for stock and flow.
- Interpretation and methodology: Reporting follows the CRR “consolidated situation” (different from IFRS consolidation for insurance, JVs, subsidiaries). Swedbank engages in industry work (Swedish Bankers’ Association) to interpret evolving guidance and continues to refine reporting processes and internal controls; denominators for tables are specified (e.g., Total GAR assets).

structure.title: Development of Taxonomy reporting
structure.heading: Development of Taxonomy reporting
structure.start_phrase: Swedbank is subject to the EU Taxonomy Regulation, a classification system that defines the criteria used to determine when economic activities, that are eligible for the EU Taxonomy, can be considered environmentally sustainable.
structure.summary:
- Context and scope: Swedbank reports under the EU Taxonomy Regulation, outlining criteria for environmental sustainability (substantial contribution to one of six objectives, do no significant harm, minimum social safeguards, and technical screening criteria).
- Reporting evolution: Since 2021 Swedbank has reported Taxonomy-eligible assets; in 2023 alignment reporting for climate objectives was added for credit institutions; in 2024 eligibility reporting expands to the remaining four environmental objectives. A new consolidated, segment‑weighted KPI (banking, asset management, insurance) is introduced, with new detailed tables for insurance and asset managers. Non‑financial activities are not aligned but included in the consolidated KPI. Fees/commissions and the trading book will be added to the consolidated KPI in 2025.
- Segment and consolidation treatment: Asset manager table covers Swedbank Robur AB and subsidiaries and provides detail beyond the credit institutions’ AuM line. Life insurance includes Robur‑managed holdings. In credit institution tables, insurance subs are reported as equities in non‑NFRD/CSRD companies (equity method). Detailed EU Taxonomy tables are referenced (pages 144–226).
- Key results as of 31 Dec 2024:
  - Green Asset Ratio (GAR) stock: 3.37% (turnover) and 3.59% (capex); aligned assets SEK 64 290m (turnover) and SEK 68 504m (capex). Increases driven by better data quality (more mortgage loans shown as aligned) and improved KPIs from NFRD/CSRD companies; inclusion of all six objectives has a positive, though smaller, effect.
  - GAR flow: 3.08% (turnover) and 3.15% (capex); aligned flow SEK 8 412m (turnover) and SEK 8 646m (capex).
  - Asset management green ratio (stock): 1.38% (turnover; SEK 32 571m) and 2.23% (capex; SEK 52 450m). Denominator changed to total AuM, lowering KPIs versus prior year; 2023 restated. Alignment increased with inclusion of financial institutions and all six objectives.
  - Asset management green ratio (flow, first year reported): 1.20% (turnover; SEK 8 299m) and 1.75% (capex; SEK 12 126m).
  - Consolidated KPIs: 3.05% (turnover) and 3.38% (capex).
  - Gas and nuclear KPIs: mostly 0.00%, at most 0.70% for both turnover and capex.
- Data considerations: Reported Taxonomy alignment data remains limited but is expected to improve, affecting both stock and flow KPIs over time.
- Methodology and interpretation: Reporting follows the CRR consolidated situation (differs from IFRS consolidation for insurance, JVs, subsidiaries), with otherwise consistent principles. Swedbank is implementing ongoing EU guidance, engaging via the Swedish Bankers’ Association, and strengthening internal controls. In credit institution tables 3–4, the KPI denominator is Total GAR assets (Total gross carrying amount), while total assets are used for the coverage proportion. Definitions are referenced (page 381), and segment breakdowns for aligned assets are noted (page 78).

structure.title: KPIs
structure.heading: KPIs
structure.start_phrase: The main KPI for banks, the Green Asset Ratio in stock (GAR), aims to increase transparency and accelerate the sustainable transition.
structure.summary:
- Overview of Swedbank’s EU Taxonomy reporting: purpose, eligibility vs. alignment criteria, and the EU’s six environmental objectives.
- Expansion of reporting in 2023–2024: inclusion of alignment metrics for credit institutions (turnover and capex), extension to all six environmental objectives for eligibility, and first-time consolidated KPI across banking, asset management, and insurance weighted by segment net income.
- Methodology updates: introduction of detailed tables for insurance and asset management; scope clarifications (e.g., insurance holdings via equity method in credit institution tables; Robur included for asset management); non-financial activities not aligned but included in the consolidated KPI; fees/commissions and trading book to be added to the consolidated KPI from 2025.
- Key performance indicators and 2024 results:
  - Green Asset Ratio (GAR) stock: 3.37% (turnover) and 3.59% (capex); alignment increased to SEK 64,290m (turnover) and SEK 68,504m (capex).
  - GAR flow: 3.08% (turnover) and 3.15% (capex); alignment of SEK 8,412m (turnover) and SEK 8,646m (capex).
  - Asset management “green ratio” stock: 1.38% (turnover) and 2.23% (capex); alignment of SEK 32,571m (turnover) and SEK 52,450m (capex). Denominator changed to total AUM, lowering KPIs vs. prior method; 2023 figures restated.
  - Asset management flow (first-time): 1.20% (turnover) and 1.75% (capex); alignment of SEK 8,299m (turnover) and SEK 12,126m (capex).
  - Consolidated KPIs: 3.05% (turnover) and 3.38% (capex).
  - Gas and nuclear KPIs: mostly 0.00%, max 0.70%.
- Drivers of improvements: better data quality enabling more household mortgage alignment; improved KPIs from NFRD/CSRD companies; inclusion of all six environmental objectives; inclusion of financial institutions in asset management alignment.
- Data and reporting notes: data availability remains limited but expected to improve; detailed segment tables referenced; denominators clarified (e.g., Total GAR assets for certain tables).
- Interpretation and governance: reporting based on CRR consolidated situation (differs from IFRS consolidation scope); ongoing implementation of evolving EU guidance; active participation in industry discussions; continued enhancement of processes and internal controls.

structure.title: Interpretation and implementation
structure.heading: Interpretation and implementation
structure.start_phrase: EU Taxonomy reporting is based on the consolidated situation as defined in Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 of the European Parliament and the Council on prudential requirements for credit institutions.
structure.summary:
- Purpose and framework: Explains Swedbank’s EU Taxonomy reporting, the criteria for alignment (substantial contribution, do no significant harm, minimum safeguards, technical screening), and the Taxonomy’s role in financing sustainable growth.

- Reporting development and scope:
  - Since 2021: reporting of Taxonomy-eligible assets.
  - 2023: expanded to Taxonomy-aligned disclosure for credit institutions (climate objectives) and assets under management (AUM).
  - 2024: eligibility expanded to all six environmental objectives; first-time introduction of a consolidated KPI weighted by business segments (banking, asset management, insurance) by share of Group net income; first-time detailed tables for insurance and asset management.
  - 2025: fees, commissions and trading book to be included in consolidated KPI.
  - Non-financial activities are not Taxonomy-aligned but are included in the consolidated KPI denominator.
  - Separate standardised tables provided for credit institutions, asset management, insurance, and activities in nuclear and fossil gas; additional consolidated KPIs by segment.

- Key KPIs and results (as of 31 Dec 2024):
  - Green Asset Ratio (GAR) – stock: 3.37% (turnover), 3.59% (capex); aligned assets SEK 64,290m (turnover) and SEK 68,504m (capex).
  - GAR – flow: 3.08% (turnover), 3.15% (capex); aligned flow SEK 8,412m (turnover) and SEK 8,646m (capex).
  - AUM green ratio – stock: 1.38% (turnover), 2.23% (capex); aligned assets SEK 32,571m (turnover) and SEK 52,450m (capex). Denominator changed to total AUM, lowering KPIs vs prior year; 2023 figures restated.
  - AUM green ratio – flow (first-time): 1.20% (turnover), 1.75% (capex); aligned flow SEK 8,299m (turnover) and SEK 12,126m (capex).
  - Consolidated KPIs: 3.05% (turnover), 3.38% (capex).
  - Gas and nuclear KPIs mostly 0.00%, at most 0.70% for turnover/capex.
  - Increases mainly driven by better data quality (especially mortgages), inclusion of all six environmental objectives, and improved KPIs from NFRD/CSRD companies; inclusion of financial institutions’ alignment in AUM also contributed.

- Methodology, interpretation and governance:
  - Reporting based on the “consolidated situation” under CRR (EU 575/2013), which differs from IFRS consolidation for certain entities; otherwise consistent principles.
  - Denominators: in credit institution tables 3–4, Total GAR assets (total gross carrying amount) for KPI calculations; “proportion of total assets covered” uses total assets.
  - Ongoing implementation work, interpretation clarifications, internal controls, and participation in industry working groups (Swedish Bankers’ Association).
  - Quarterly monitoring of alignment/KPIs by Business Areas; updates to customer processes and products to evidence loan-level alignment.
  - Climate strategy linkage: increasing Taxonomy-aligned assets supports 2030 financed emissions targets (e.g., commercial properties, mortgages); some funds commit to minimum Taxonomy alignment; Taxonomy used as a key tool in asset management and for climate targets.

- Loans collateralised by residential immovable property:
  - Largest source of Taxonomy-eligible assets; energy efficiency in housing is central to emissions reduction.
  - Alignment criteria differ by build date:
    - Pre-31 Dec 2020: within top 15% primary energy or energy class A.
    - Post-31 Dec 2020: at least 10% below NZEB threshold.
  - DNSH for climate adaptation assessed via climate risk assessments (aligned with Pillar 3 methodology); external data provider used; both energy compliance and low climate risk required.
  - Swedish thresholds based on Fastighetsägarna; analogous approach in Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania.

- Dependence on NFRD/CSRD company data:
  - Financial institutions rely on counterparties’ Taxonomy reporting; external provider used to source corporates’ data.
  - Corporate lending: 24% of assets, but only 2% are NFRD/CSRD reporters, limiting alignment.
  - AUM: 35% invested in NFRD/CSRD companies; global/ex-EU and small/mid-cap strategies reduce alignment.

- Data availability and quality challenges:
  - No central database; external data gaps/quality issues for corporate KPIs and property energy data; lack of “use of proceeds” data for loans.
  - 55% of mortgages lack valid energy performance certificates; non-harmonised energy classes (Sweden stricter for class A) hinder alignment.
  - Incomplete identification of new assets in flow denominators leads to overstated flow GAR.
  - Data expected to improve over time, affecting stock and flow KPIs.

structure.title: Loans collateralised by residential immovable property
structure.heading: Loans collateralised by residential immovable property
structure.start_phrase: The acquisition and ownership of property by households is an activity covered by the EU Taxonomy.
structure.summary:
- Swedbank monitors EU Taxonomy KPIs quarterly across Business Areas and aims to improve them by supporting customers’ sustainable operations, energy‑efficient housing, and sustainable investments.
- The bank is updating customer processes and developing products to evidence Taxonomy alignment at the individual loan level, with a focus on increasing environmentally sustainable assets and meeting 2030 financed‑emissions targets in sectors like commercial real estate and mortgages.
- In asset management, several funds commit to minimum proportions of Taxonomy‑aligned investments; the Taxonomy is a key tool for sustainability monitoring and for achieving climate targets.
- Reporting follows EU‑standardized tables for credit institutions, asset management, insurance, and activities related to nuclear energy and fossil gas, plus consolidated, segment‑weighted KPIs for banking, asset management, and insurance.
- Detailed disclosures are provided for six nuclear and fossil gas activities, including GAR, Green ratio for assets under management, Green ratio for financial guarantees, and Green ratio for life insurance AUM.
- Loans collateralised by residential property constitute most of Swedbank’s Taxonomy‑eligible assets; the bank finances energy‑efficiency improvements and relies on high‑quality energy data.
- Alignment criteria for residential collateral vary by building age:
  - Built before 31 Dec 2020: primary energy within top 15% of national stock or energy class A.
  - Built after 31 Dec 2020: primary energy at least 10% below nearly‑zero energy building thresholds.
- Swedbank applies Swedish thresholds from Fastighetsägarna and corresponding data in Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania; it conducts climate risk assessments (per Pillar 3 methodology) to meet Do No Significant Harm for Climate Change Adaptation. Loans are aligned only if energy criteria and low climate risk are both met; external data is used, with ongoing improvements.
- Swedbank’s Taxonomy reporting depends on counterparties’ NFRD/CSRD disclosures; current coverage is limited:
  - Corporate lending is 24% of assets; only 2% are NFRD/CSRD reporters.
  - 35% of AUM is in NFRD/CSRD companies; global, non‑EU, and small/mid‑cap strategies reduce alignment.
- Data constraints hinder alignment and KPI accuracy:
  - No central external database and variable data quality for customer KPIs and property energy performance.
  - Missing “use of proceeds” data for some corporate loans.
  - 55% of residential mortgage collateral lacks valid energy performance certificates, limiting proof of alignment.
  - Non‑harmonized energy class systems (stricter class A in Sweden) depress alignment.
  - Incomplete flow denominator data leads to inaccuracies and an overstated flow GAR.
- Overall, increasing Taxonomy‑aligned assets and AUM is central to meeting Swedbank’s climate targets, with ongoing efforts to enhance data, processes, and product offerings to support alignment and reporting.

structure.title: NFRD/CSRD companies
structure.heading: NFRD/CSRD companies
structure.start_phrase: Financial companies rely heavily on customers and counterparties reporting in accordance with the EU Taxonomy, so that they can fulfil their own reporting obligations.
structure.summary:
- Swedbank monitors EU Taxonomy alignment and related KPIs quarterly, aiming to improve them by supporting customers’ sustainable operations, energy‑efficient housing, and sustainable investments. The bank is updating customer processes and developing products to evidence loan‑level Taxonomy alignment, while targeting a higher share of environmentally sustainable assets and setting 2030 financed‑emissions targets in sectors like commercial property and mortgages.
- In asset management, several funds commit to a minimum share of Taxonomy‑aligned investments; the Taxonomy is a core tool for sustainability monitoring and for meeting the Group’s climate targets.
- The bank reports EU Taxonomy metrics in standardized tables for credit institutions, asset management, insurance, and activities related to nuclear energy and fossil gas, and provides consolidated KPIs for banking, asset management, and insurance weighted by each segment’s share of net income. Detailed tables cover six identified nuclear and fossil gas activities, including GAR and Green ratios for AUM, guarantees, and life insurance.
- Loans collateralised by residential property comprise the majority of Taxonomy‑eligible assets. Alignment criteria differ by construction date: pre‑2021 buildings must be in the top 15% for primary energy or have energy class A; post‑2020 buildings must be at least 10% below the nearly‑zero energy building threshold. Swedbank applies Swedish thresholds from Fastighetsägarna and comparable data for Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania.
- To meet Do No Significant Harm for Climate Change Adaptation, Swedbank conducts climate risk assessments (per its Pillar 3 methodology) on collateral; loans are Taxonomy‑aligned only if energy criteria are met and climate risk is low. External data providers are used, with ongoing improvements planned.
- Reliance on NFRD/CSRD company disclosures affects Swedbank’s alignment and eligibility figures; data from corporate sustainability statements is sourced externally. As reporting expands, data quality and availability should improve and influence alignment levels.
- Portfolio context: corporate lending is 24% of assets, but only 2% are to NFRD/CSRD reporters. In AUM, 35% is invested in NFRD/CSRD companies. Global non‑EU exposures and small/mid‑cap strategies lower overall Taxonomy alignment.
- Data gaps and quality issues hinder KPI accuracy: no central external database, limited “use of proceeds” data for corporate loans, and insufficient property energy data. For 55% of residential mortgage collateral, no valid energy performance certificate is available, constraining proof of alignment. Non‑harmonized energy classes (with stricter Swedish thresholds) further limit alignment. Incomplete flow‑denominator data reduces KPI accuracy and results in a higher reported flow GAR.

structure.title: Data availability and quality
structure.heading: Data availability and quality
structure.start_phrase: The absence of a central external database and the continued inadequate quality of external data pose difficulties in collecting quality-assured data regarding KPIs from corporate customers and energy performance for properties used as collat-eral.
structure.summary:
- Swedbank’s EU Taxonomy alignment and KPIs are monitored quarterly across business areas, with a stated ambition to improve KPIs by supporting sustainable customer activities, energy‑efficient housing, and sustainable investments.
- The bank is updating customer processes and developing products to evidence Taxonomy alignment at individual loan level, aiming to increase the share of environmentally sustainable assets; 2030 financed‑emissions targets are set for several sectors, including commercial real estate and mortgages.
- In asset management, selected funds commit to minimum proportions of Taxonomy‑aligned investments; the Taxonomy is a key monitoring tool and a lever to meet Group climate targets.
- EU Taxonomy reporting follows standardized templates for credit institutions, asset management, insurance, and activities related to nuclear energy and fossil gas, plus consolidated, income‑weighted KPIs by business segment (banking, asset management, insurance).
- Dedicated tables disclose details for six nuclear/fossil gas activities, covering GAR (Green Asset Ratio), Green ratio for assets under management (including life insurance), and Green ratio for financial guarantees.
- Loans collateralised by residential property constitute the majority of Taxonomy‑eligible assets; alignment criteria depend on building age (pre‑2021: top 15% energy performance or energy class A; post‑2020: ≥10% below nearly‑zero energy building threshold).
- DNSH for climate adaptation is assessed via climate risk analyses of residential collateral; loans are counted as aligned only when both energy criteria and low climate risk are met; data is sourced from an external provider, with ongoing improvements.
- Reporting relies on NFRD/CSRD company disclosures; currently only a small share of corporate lending (2% of corporate assets) is to reporting entities, while 35% of AUM is in reporting companies; non‑EU/global and small/mid‑cap exposures reduce overall alignment, expected to improve as CSRD expands.
- Data availability and quality are key constraints: no central database, missing or inconsistent external data (e.g., “use of proceeds”), non‑harmonised EPC systems, and 55% of residential mortgages lacking valid EPCs; incomplete flow denominators inflate the flow GAR and reduce KPI accuracy.
- E1 Climate change section outlines mitigation, adaptation, and energy across the value chain (lending, asset management, own operations), with climate deemed material throughout; it references the double materiality process (IRO‑1).
- Swedbank’s Climate Transition Plan, aligned with its business strategy, targets net‑zero by 2050 and 1.5°C‑aligned sector pathways by 2030; it emphasizes steering lending and investments via engagement, advice, and product development.
- Fossil‑related restrictions: no new financing for companies extracting oil, gas, thermal coal or peat (limited exceptions for defined transition cases); no dedicated financing for coal/peat power, new oil/gas power plants, oil tankers, or refineries; investment exclusions for companies with >5% revenue from fossil extraction or fossil‑based power (with narrow transition exceptions; indirect third‑party funds/discretionary mandates excluded).
- Lending focus in the transition plan is the real estate sector (~80% of loan exposure), with actions to support customers’ transition, build partnerships, and scale financing of sustainable activities; the plan is CEO‑approved, Board‑reviewed, and will be updated to reflect CSRD/CSDDD.

structure.title: Introduction
structure.heading: Introduction
structure.start_phrase: E1 Climate change covers Swedbank’s reporting relating to climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation and energy.
structure.summary:
- Scope and structure: The E1 Climate change section reports on climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, and energy across Swedbank’s full value chain. It is divided into three areas—Lending, Asset management (Swedbank Robur Fonder), and Own operations—reflecting the double materiality assessment. Climate is material upstream, in own operations, and downstream, with differing methods, targets, and metrics per area.  
- Materiality and IRO linkage: Impacts, risks, and opportunities (positive and negative) are identified across the value chain, with cross-references to the Group’s process for identifying and assessing material IROs (IRO-1).  
- Strategy and transition plan: Sustainability is integrated into business strategy, with a Group-wide commitment to net-zero emissions by 2050 and alignment with the 1.5°C pathway. Swedbank has published a Climate Transition Plan, emphasizing the lending portfolio where most climate impact occurs, and prioritizing customer transition support. The plan is approved by the CEO, reviewed by the Board, and will be updated in line with CSRD and CSDDD.  
- Targets:  
  - Lending: Six sector-specific 2030 climate targets aligned with 1.5°C reduction trajectories, focusing especially on the real estate sector (about 80% of loan exposure).  
  - Asset management: Climate targets for fund management aligned with the 1.5°C pathway.  
  - Own operations: Covers direct operational impacts such as energy use, travel, and procurement (details implied to be elsewhere).  
- Portfolio steering and client engagement: Swedbank aims to steer financing and investments toward sustainable activities through engagement, advice, tailored financial solutions, monitoring, and partnerships to enable customers’ transition.  
- Fossil fuel position and exclusions:  
  - Lending/financing: No new financing or capital market financing to companies extracting oil, gas, thermal coal, or thermal peat; no dedicated financing for coal/peat power generation or for companies with over 5% revenue from these; no dedicated financing for new oil or gas power plants, new oil tankers, or new oil refineries. Limited exceptions may be granted for transition companies (with criteria) or in extraordinary circumstances, with an expectation of Paris-aligned transition plans.  
  - Investments: Exclusion of companies with more than 5% of revenues from extraction or power generation from oil, gas, thermal coal, or thermal peat, with possible exceptions for transition companies. Indirect investments (third-party funds, discretionary mandates) are not covered.  
- Implementation actions to 2030:  
  - Support and engage customers to stimulate transition with adapted solutions and advice.  
  - Develop partnerships and collaborations to aid customer transition.  
  - Increase financing of sustainable and transition-enabling activities.

structure.title: Transition plan
structure.heading: Transition plan, E1-1
structure.start_phrase: Sustainability is at the heart of Swedbank’s business strategy, which means that sustainability aspects are integrated into the Group’s work and business deci-sions.
structure.summary:
- Scope and structure: The E1 Climate change section covers Swedbank’s reporting on climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, and energy across the entire value chain (upstream, own operations, downstream). It is organized into three areas—Lending, Asset management (Swedbank Robur Fonder), and Own operations—reflecting the bank’s double materiality assessment. Methods, targets, and metrics differ by area. References are made to IRO-1 for the process of identifying material impacts, risks, and opportunities.

- Strategy and transition plan (E1-1): Sustainability is embedded in Swedbank’s business strategy, with a Group-wide Climate Transition Plan aligned to a net-zero by 2050 objective and the 1.5°C pathway. The plan emphasizes the bank’s role as a systemic institution in enabling customer transition, given that the largest climate impact occurs through customers. Swedbank has set six sector-specific 2030 climate targets for its lending portfolio and climate targets for fund management aligned with 1.5°C, steering financing and investments via dialogue, advice, and monitoring.

- Fossil fuel stance and restrictions: Swedbank’s Position Statement on Climate Change and Nature restricts new financing or capital market financing to companies extracting oil, gas, thermal coal, or thermal peat, with limited exceptions for defined “transition companies” or extraordinary cases requiring Paris-aligned transition plans. The bank will not provide dedicated financing to coal/peat power generation or to companies with over 5% revenue from these, nor to new oil/gas power plants, oil tankers, or oil refineries. For investments, companies with more than 5% revenue from fossil extraction or power generation are excluded, with narrow exceptions for transition cases; indirect investments (third-party funds/discretionary mandates) are not covered.

- Lending focus and actions: The Climate Transition Plan for lending (approved by the CEO and reviewed by the Board) sets out how Swedbank will reach net zero in its lending portfolio and increase sustainable financing. It will be updated to align with evolving climate work and regulations (CSDDD, CSRD). Priority is the green energy transition in the real estate sector, which constitutes ~80% of loan exposure. Key actions include:
  - Supporting and engaging customers with tailored financing and advice.
  - Building partnerships and collaborations to aid customer transition.
  - Increasing financing of sustainable and transition-contributing activities.

nodes.title: Lending
nodes.heading: Lending
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank’s published transition plan aims to describe how Swedbank is working towards the net-zero target in Swedbank’s lending portfolio as well as the ambition to increase sustainable financing volumes.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and structure: The E1 Climate change section covers climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, and energy across Swedbank’s entire value chain (upstream, own operations, downstream). Reporting is organized into three areas: Lending, Asset management (Swedbank Robur Fonder), and Own operations (e.g., energy use, travel, IT/office purchases). Climate change is assessed as material in all value chain divisions, with methods, targets, and metrics tailored per area. References are made to the materiality process in IRO-1.

- Strategy and transition plan (E1-1): Sustainability is embedded in Swedbank’s business strategy and underpins the Group’s Climate Transition Plan, which is aligned with limiting warming to 1.5°C and achieving net-zero emissions by 2050. The plan emphasizes steering lending and investment portfolios, sets six sector-specific 2030 climate targets for the loan portfolio, and includes climate targets for fund management. The plan prioritizes enabling customer transition, given the largest impacts occur via customers. It was approved by the CEO, reviewed by the Board, and will be updated in line with developments and requirements under CSDDD and CSRD.

- Fossil fuel position and exclusions: Swedbank will not provide new financing or capital market financing to companies extracting oil, gas, thermal coal, or thermal peat, with limited exceptions for defined transition companies or extraordinary cases requiring Paris-aligned transition plans. The bank will not provide dedicated financing to coal/peat power generation or to companies with more than 5% revenue from these activities, nor to new oil/gas power plants, new oil tankers, or new oil refineries. For investments, companies with more than 5% revenue from extraction or power generation from oil, gas, thermal coal, or thermal peat are excluded, with possible exceptions for transition companies; indirect investments (third-party funds/discretionary mandates) are not covered.

- Lending portfolio focus: The transition plan details how Swedbank will progress toward net zero in its lending portfolio and increase sustainable financing. Primary focus is on the real estate sector, which represents about 80% of loan exposure. Integrated 2030 credit portfolio targets align with a 1.5°C pathway. Key actions include: engaging and advising customers to stimulate transition; developing partnerships to support customer transition; and increasing financing of sustainable and transition-enabling activities.

- Cross-references and next steps: Additional details on targets appear in E1-4 and on materiality in IRO-1. The section maps climate-related impacts, risks, and opportunities across the value chain and underscores that climate work is Group-wide while being executed with area-specific tools and metrics.

nodes.title: Drivers in the transition
nodes.heading: Drivers in the transition
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank has multiple opportunities to contribute to the phasing out of fossil fuels and the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions.
nodes.summary:
- Swedbank’s role in the climate transition centers on sustainable financing, advice, and awareness across its broad customer base, with priority on the real estate sector and other high-emission areas (power generation, oil and gas, shipping, steel).
- Business drivers include partnerships in green technology, rising market demand for green financial products, investor expectations, and tightening regulation; however, Swedbank is not yet conducting quantitative analysis of emission-reduction drivers.
- The bank aims to reduce exposure to customers unwilling to transition, guided by its Position Statement on Climate Change and Nature; it identifies potential locked-in emissions in fossil-intensive sectors and has set 2030 climate targets for these sectors, emphasizing engagement, advice, and monitoring.
- Tools were developed to assess corporate customers’ transition plans, informing internal decisions and client advice; achieving group climate targets depends on customers’ emissions trajectories and risk management, as well as Swedbank’s sector exposures.
- The Climate Transition Plan is not embedded in financial planning; no separate operating or capital expenditures are identified for the plan, and 2024 serves as the baseline year with no measurable results yet (further actions referenced in Actions, E1-3; sector targets in Targets, E1-4).
- Asset management: Swedbank Robur Fonder’s climate strategy and Responsible Investment Policy (board-approved, annually revised) guide net-zero alignment; as an NZAM signatory, it targets net-zero by 2040 (ahead of Paris 2050) via investing in transition solutions, active ownership to drive net-zero, exclusions that conflict with the strategy, and fulfilling external commitments and reporting.
- Own operations: target to reduce direct GHG emissions by 60% by 2030 versus 2019 (covering scope 1, scope 2, and selected scope 3); alignment with 1.5°C has not been evaluated.
- Strategy and business model: Swedbank sees both risk and opportunity, with its largest climate impact occurring through customers and investments; it aims to lead in financing sustainable solutions, especially energy efficiency in buildings, but cannot yet assess the effects/resources of listed measures.
- Climate-related risks are primarily indirect and dominated by transition risk; sectors with significant exposure include energy, property management, transport, forestry and agriculture, and manufacturing. Examples of credit risk drivers include stricter building energy regulations (potential property devaluation and cash flow impacts), disruptive low-carbon technologies and electrification (competitiveness risks for laggards), and shifting consumer/investor preferences toward sustainable products (demand and valuation impacts).

nodes.title: Asset management
nodes.heading: Asset management
nodes.start_phrase: The Swedbank Climate Transition Plan describes the Group’s overall approach to achieving net-zero emissions in fund management, which is described in more detail in Swedbank Robur Fonder’s climate strategy.
nodes.summary:
- Swedbank’s transition role centers on sustainable financing, advice, and awareness, leveraging its broad customer base to phase out fossil fuels and cut greenhouse gas emissions.
- Priority sectors include real estate (a major exposure across home markets) and other emission-intensive sectors—power generation, oil and gas, shipping, and steel—given their significant share of financed emissions.
- Key drivers: partnerships and business opportunities in green technology, rising customer demand for green financial products, evolving investor expectations, and tightening regulation; however, Swedbank is not yet performing quantitative analysis or follow-up on drivers of emissions reductions.
- Portfolio alignment approach includes reducing exposure to customers unwilling to transition, guided by Swedbank’s Position Statement on Climate Change and Nature; “locked-in” emissions are concentrated in fossil- and carbon-intensive assets, with 2030 climate targets set for priority sectors and active client dialogue, advice, and monitoring.
- The bank’s ability to meet sector targets depends on clients’ transition progress and Swedbank’s exposure levels; 2024 is a baseline year, so no measurable results are reported yet.
- Transition planning is not embedded in financial planning; no distinct transition-related capex/opex is identified, as costs are included in ongoing operations.
- Tools were developed to assess corporate clients’ transition plans, informing internal decisions and client advisory; achieving group targets depends on clients’ emissions trajectories, adaptability, and climate risk management.
- Asset management: Swedbank Robur Fonder’s climate strategy and Responsible Investment Policy (board-approved and annually revised) guide net-zero alignment; as an NZAM signatory, Robur targets net-zero by 2040 and pursues four levers—meeting external commitments, investing in transition solutions, engaging to drive net-zero, and excluding activities that hinder the strategy.
- Own operations: target a 60% reduction in direct GHG emissions by 2030 vs. 2019 across scope 1, scope 2, and selected scope 3 categories; alignment with a 1.5°C pathway has not been evaluated.
- Strategy and business model: Swedbank aims to lead the green transition, focusing on financing sustainable solutions—especially energy efficiency in buildings—recognizing both risks and significant business opportunities; effects/resources of listed measures are not yet assessed.
- Climate risk management: transition risk is the most material and largely indirect via lending and investments; high-risk sectors include energy, property management, transport, forestry and agriculture, and manufacturing.
- Examples of transition risk events increasing credit risk: stricter building energy-efficiency rules affecting property cash flows/values; rapid tech shifts (e.g., energy, transport electrification) disadvantaging laggards; consumer/investor preference shifts reducing demand and risk appetite for unsustainable business models.

nodes.title: Own operations
nodes.heading: Own operations
nodes.start_phrase: Own operations are covered by Swedbank’s transition plan.
nodes.summary:
- Swedbank’s role in the climate transition centers on sustainable financing, advice, and awareness, leveraging its broad customer base.
- Strategic focus on enabling energy transition in real estate and other emission-intensive sectors (power generation, oil and gas, shipping, steel) due to their significant share of financed emissions.
- Business drivers include growing demand for green financial products, evolving investor expectations, regulatory requirements, and partnerships in green technology; however, no quantitative analysis of emission-reduction drivers is conducted yet.
- Commitment to reduce exposure to customers with low transition willingness, guided by the Position Statement on Climate Change and Nature; recognition of potentially locked-in emissions in fossil- and carbon-intensive sectors.
- Sector-specific 2030 climate targets for oil and gas, power generation, steel, and shipping, with active customer dialogue, advisory, and monitoring; progress depends on customers’ transition capacity and Swedbank’s sectoral exposure.
- Development of tools to assess corporate customers’ transition plans, feeding into internal decisions and client advisory.
- The Climate Transition Plan is not integrated into financial planning; no distinct transition-related capex/opex identified; 2024 set as baseline year with no measurable results yet.
- Asset management (Swedbank Robur Fonder): governed by a Board-approved responsible investment policy and climate strategy; NZAM signatory; ambition to be ahead of global timelines (net-zero by 2040); approach includes aligning with Paris goals, investing in transition solutions, active ownership to influence holdings, and exclusions where necessary.
- Own operations target: 60% reduction in direct GHG emissions by 2030 vs. 2019 (scopes 1, 2, and selected scope 3); 1.5°C alignment not yet evaluated.
- Strategy and business model are being adapted to climate impacts, risks, and opportunities, with emphasis on financing sustainable solutions and boosting building energy efficiency; largest climate impact arises via customers and investments.
- Climate risk management: risks largely indirect through lending and investments; transition risk deemed most material, especially in energy, property management, transport, forestry/agriculture, and manufacturing.
- Examples of transition risk drivers increasing credit risk: tighter building efficiency regulations reducing property cash flows/values; rapid technological shifts and electrification challenging unprepared firms; changing consumer/investor preferences decreasing demand and risk appetite for less sustainable businesses.

structure.title: Strategy and business model
structure.heading: Strategy and business model, E1, SBM-3
structure.start_phrase: Swedbank believes that it is important to adapt its strategy and business model to the identified impacts, risks and opportunities in the climate area.
structure.summary:
- Swedbank’s role in the climate transition centers on sustainable financing, advisory, and awareness-raising across its broad customer base, with growing opportunities driven by green technology, partnerships, market demand for green products, investor expectations, and tightening regulation.
- Strategic sector focus on high-emitting industries—real estate, power generation, oil and gas, shipping, and steel—due to their significant share of financed emissions; climate targets set for 2030 in these sectors and active client dialogue, advice, and monitoring.
- Emphasis on reducing exposure to customers unwilling or unable to transition; expectations and fossil-fuel restrictions defined in Swedbank’s Position Statement on Climate Change and Nature.
- Recognition of potentially locked-in emissions in fossil-intensive assets; progress toward targets depends on clients’ transition capabilities and Swedbank’s sector exposure.
- Development of tools to assess corporate clients’ transition plans to inform internal decisions and client advice; no quantitative analysis yet on specific emission-reduction drivers.
- Transition plan is not integrated into financial planning; no distinct capex/opex earmarked—costs treated as part of ongoing operations.
- 2024 is the baseline year; no measurable transition results reported for the year; additional actions referenced in other sections.
- Asset management: Swedbank Robur Fonder’s climate strategy (under Board-approved Responsible Investment Policy) guides net-zero alignment; signatory to NZAM; targets more ambitious than global timelines (net zero by 2040 vs 2050); approach includes investing in transition solutions, active ownership to drive decarbonization, exclusions, and transparent reporting.
- Own operations: target to cut direct GHG emissions by 60% by 2030 vs 2019 (Scopes 1, 2, and selected Scope 3); 1.5°C alignment of this target not evaluated.

- Climate risk management: transition risk deemed most material; key exposed sectors include energy, property management, transport, forestry/agriculture, and manufacturing.
- Illustrative transition risk drivers and credit risk implications:
  - Policy/regulation (e.g., EU building efficiency rules) potentially reducing cash flows and asset values for low-performing properties.

nodes.title: Resilience analysis through scenario analysis and stress tests
nodes.heading: Resilience analysis through scenario analysis and stress tests
nodes.start_phrase: Based on the scenario analysis and the stress tests conducted as part of Swedbank’s Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP), the conclusion is that the Group’s resilience to climate-related risks is good.
nodes.summary:
- ICAAP climate resilience assessment: Ten-year baseline scenario and three-year stress tests (covering transition and physical risks like flooding) indicate Swedbank has good resilience; profitability and capitalisation remain strong in the baseline.
- Scope and methodology: Analysis covers the consolidated Group and downstream value chain (excluding wholly owned insurance companies, included only as shareholdings); upstream value chain not included; no significant transition risks excluded; processes are new and under development.
- Key assumptions: Macroeconomy follows long-term trend; substantial investment needs across home markets, especially in energy (shift to renewables, notably in the Baltics) and transport (electrification); no explicit energy consumption assumption; longer horizon increases uncertainty around portfolio, income, and expenses.
- Identified challenge: Property financing may constrain achievement of financed emissions targets, as customer energy-efficiency actions are partly outside the bank’s control; further detail in the Transition Plan (E1-1).
- Governance and policy framework: Sustainability Policy, Environmental Policy, Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) Policy, and Credit Policy guide climate-related risk management; ESG risk defined as a separate risk type, with climate risks as key drivers of credit and operational risks; ESG integrated into credit assessment, monitoring, and directives.
- Position Statement on Climate Change and Nature: Commits to climate mitigation and adaptation, active financing of transition, customer support, and promotion of enabling technologies (electrification, renewables); sets targets, integrates climate risk into analyses, and imposes fossil fuel restrictions; governance documents available internally and publicly.
- Actions (E1-3): Yearly measures to reduce emissions include partnerships, strengthened governance, and clarified targets; focus on directing financial flows to sustainable activities and supporting customer transition through advice and services; no significant standalone sustainability opex/capex—costs are embedded in operations.
- Enablers and dependencies: Effective climate action relies on access to capital, internal sustainability expertise, and high-quality data for strategy, risk identification, decisions, and tracking progress; the Group is highly dependent on these resources.
- Impact and reach: Negative impacts are recognized and targeted for reduction, though stakeholder coverage cannot be precisely quantified; further progress expected via new products, services, and tools, with emphasis on the real estate sector.
- Highlighted measure: Publication of Swedbank’s Climate Transition Plan, detailing emissions reduction approach, alignment with international commitments, financing of the societal transition, and a key focus on energy-efficiency improvements in real estate.

nodes.title: Publication of Swedbank’s Climate Transition Plan
nodes.heading: Publication of Swedbank’s Climate Transition Plan
nodes.start_phrase: The preparation and publication of the Climate Transition Plan, which describes the Group’s climate work and highlights the most important elements, was a key mea - sure during the year.
nodes.summary:
- ICAAP scenario and stress testing conclude Swedbank has good resilience to climate-related risks, including stressed transition risks and severe flooding scenarios.
- Analysis framework includes a 10-year baseline transition scenario (aligned with the bank’s climate targets) showing strong profitability and capitalisation, and 3-year macro stress tests integrating physical and transition risks.
- Scope covers the consolidated Group and downstream value chain (excluding wholly owned insurance companies beyond shareholdings); upstream value chain not included.
- Processes and methodologies for the scenarios are new and evolving; results rely on assumptions about long-term macro trends and increased investment needs, notably in renewable energy (especially Baltics) and transport electrification; heightened uncertainty over longer horizons.
- Key challenge identified: property financing and reliance on customers’ energy-efficiency measures to meet financed-emission targets.
- Governance: multiple policies guide climate risk and impact management—Sustainability Policy, Environmental Policy, ERM Policy, and Credit Policy—embedding ESG (with climate risks as a focus) into risk taxonomy, credit assessment, and monitoring.
- Position Statement on Climate Change and Nature sets expectations for mitigation and adaptation, active financing of transition (e.g., electrification, renewables), transparency on climate risk, target-setting, and fossil fuel restrictions; public documents available online.
- Actions center on steering financial flows to sustainable activities, with climate-related costs embedded in ongoing operations rather than standalone capex/opex lines.
- Enablers and dependencies: access to capital, internal sustainability expertise, and high-quality data are critical to execute mitigation and adaptation strategies and track progress.
- Publication of a Climate Transition Plan prioritizing downstream financed emissions, especially energy-efficiency in real estate; plan is iterative and currently lacks granular quantitative attribution of emission reductions.
- Ambitions announced to triple sustainable financing volumes by 2027 vs. 2022 and to reach at least 40% ESG bonds in advised issuances.
- Customer solutions and partnerships to drive energy transition: digital home energy checks (Hemma), corporate advisory collaboration (Ramboll), property energy-efficiency simulation platform, agri collaborations (Agronod, eAgronom) across home markets.
- Asset management (Swedbank Robur Fonder): net-zero approach via exclusions (fossil fuels), inclusion, and active engagement; daily controls on exclusions; advocacy for SBTi targets; reduced weighted average carbon intensity and increased SBTi-verified exposure.
- Own operations: began mapping scope 3 supply-chain emissions (Purchased goods and services) to enable reduction strategies.
- Targets and metrics: climate target reporting based on 2023 customer emissions data; financed emissions reporting for 2024 uses latest available data and 2024 exposure, creating methodological differences.
- Target-setting aligned with NZBA 1.5°C sectoral trajectories; approved by CEO and reviewed by the Board; stakeholder input considered at a high level but targets not co-set with stakeholders; no quantified attribution of total emissions reductions yet.
- Six sector-specific financed-emission targets to 2030 (mostly intensity-based): mortgages, commercial real estate, power generation, oil & gas, steel, and newly added shipping; targets follow PCAF sector definitions, not third-party validated; outcomes influenced by customer emissions, portfolio exposure, and client asset sizes.

- Expanded customer offerings and partnerships to support the energy transition:
  - Retail: digital home energy checks in Sweden via Hemma.
  - Corporate: collaboration with Ramboll and a platform to simulate property energy-efficiency needs and share energy/sustainability insights.
  - Agriculture: partnerships with Agronod (farm carbon footprint reporting) and eAgronom in the Baltics (financing for sustainable agriculture).
- Asset management (Swedbank Robur Fonder): net-zero approach with fossil fuel exclusions (coal, oil, gas) and daily compliance checks; active engagement with high-emitting holdings lacking SBTi-verified targets; declining weighted average carbon intensity from 2023 to 2024 and a higher share of SBTi-verified investees.
- Own operations: 2024 review and mapping of Scope 3 purchased goods and services emissions across the supplier base to enable supply-chain reductions.
- Metrics and targets (E1-4) for lending:
