nodes.title: Health and safety metrics, S1-14
nodes.heading: 6.1.14 Health and safety metrics, S1-14
nodes.start_phrase: The table presents internally reported occupational accidents in the form of occupational accidents and work-related ill health.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Summarizes Swedbank’s 2024 approach and performance on employee training/skills development (ESRS S1-13) and health and safety metrics (ESRS S1-14), including methodologies, data sources, assumptions, and key results.

- Training and skills development (S1-13):
  - Philosophy and tools: Emphasis on self-leadership and shared responsibility for career growth. Performance Development (PD) is the core process to set individual goals and development activities aligned with Swedbank’s strategy.
  - Competence standards: High competence expectations across roles; mandatory Group-wide courses on ethics, security, anti-corruption/bribery, and AML/CFT, with a 100% participation target for mandatory training.
  - Metrics and results:
    - High participation in regular performance and career development reviews (around 91–93% in 2024, broadly in line with 2023).
    - One review per employee expected annually; total reviews conducted in 2024 were 17,657 (with gender breakdowns captured).
    - Average training hours per employee declined slightly year-on-year (total 27 hours in 2024 vs 30 in 2023; women generally higher than men).
    - Gender is measured as legal gender (Male/Female).
  - Methodology and data quality:
    - Review participation ratio covers employees with main assignments, broken down by gender.
    - Average training hours calculated as total completed hours per gender divided by total employees per gender; headcount figures align with ESRS S1-6.
    - Data sourced from HR system SABA; gaps from specific legal entities are requested from local representatives.
    - Quality checks ensure completeness (all employment types/countries) and consistency (vs prior reports).
  - Assumptions: If data is missing for certain legal entities, performance is assumed to align with overall averages.

- Health and safety metrics (S1-14):
  - Scope and exclusions: Reports occupational accidents and work-related ill health occurring at or due to work; commuting incidents are excluded.
  - Reporting system: Incidents are reported per local legislation to authorities and internally through a Group incident system following a common routine.
  - Coverage and governance: 100% of employees are covered by the Group’s health and safety system in all operating countries; subject to external reviews (e.g., Sweden’s Work Environment Authority) and annual internal audits.
  - Assumptions: For Finland, Norway, USA, China, and PayEx (not fully covered by the incident system), accident frequency is assumed equal to other parts of the Group.
  - 2024 performance (vs 2023):
    - Coverage: 100% for both employees and non-employees.
    - Fatalities: 0 for employees and others (unchanged).
    - Registered occupational accidents (employees): 25 (up from 23).
    - Accident frequency (employees): 0.90 (up from 0.82).
    - Non-employee accidents: 0.

- Cross-references: Additional detail is available in Development and learning (S1-4), Training (S4-4), Code of Conduct (G1-1), and Financial crime sections.

nodes.title: Work-life balance, S1-15
nodes.heading: 6.1.15 Work-life balance, S1-15
nodes.start_phrase: All Swedbank employees are entitled to parental leave through collective agree- ments or local legislation.
nodes.summary:
- Work-life balance and parental leave: All employees are entitled to parental leave via collective agreements or local law. Swedbank emphasizes flexibility as part of its equity and diversity work, offering part-time options for returnees, flexible hours, and offsite work when roles allow.
- Parental leave metric and scope: Measures the proportion of employees entitled to parental leave who actually took it, reported by legal gender (Male/Female) as of 31 December 2024. Additional country and gender detail is referenced in note G13.9.
- Parental leave assumptions: Employees outside home markets (5% of workforce) who are on leave on 31 December 2024 are assumed to be on parental leave; within this group, 5% of women and 2% of men are assumed to have taken leave.
- Parental leave results: 2024 vs 2023 share taking leave—Female: 16% (16%); Male: 15% (13%); Total: 16% (15%).
- Remuneration indicators purpose: Disclose gender pay gaps, CEO-to-median employee pay ratio, and equal pay for equal work gaps to assess remuneration inequality within the Group.
- Methodologies:
  - Gender pay gap: Difference between men’s and women’s gross hourly wages relative to men’s wage; scope is all Group employees; positive means men earn more.
  - CEO pay ratio: CEO’s annual total remuneration relative to the median of all employees (excluding the highest paid); scope is all Group employees.
  - Equal Pay Gap: Comparison of average salary index for men and women by job level and market in home markets; positive means men earn more.
- Data sources and quality: Data drawn from HR and finance systems; missing legal-entity data gathered from entity representatives; checks for completeness and consistency against prior reports.
- Remuneration assumptions: Where entity data is missing, assume results align with other entities. Since home markets are ~95% of the workforce, the Group median total remuneration is assumed equal to the home markets’ median.
- Reported outcomes:
  - Gender pay gap (all employees), 2024 (2023): Sweden 19% (19%); Estonia 29% (29%); Latvia 29% (30%); Lithuania 32% (33%); Swedbank Group 28% (29%).
  - CEO total remuneration ratio vs employees’ median, 2024 (2023): Group 31 (32).
  - Equal Pay Gap (equal work), 2024 (2023): Sweden 1.6% (1.9%); Estonia 0.1% (1.1%); Latvia 0.2% (0.9%); Lithuania –0.2% (0%); Total (home markets) 1.1% (1.5%).
- Clarifications: Gender is measured as legal gender (Male/Female).

structure.title: Introduction
structure.heading: 6.2.1 Introduction
structure.start_phrase: Chapter S4 Consumers and end-users concerns Swedbank’s reporting related to information-related impacts for consumers and/or end-users.
structure.summary:
- Scope: Section S4 covers Swedbank’s information-related impacts on consumers and end-users, mapped in the value chain primarily downstream (consumers/end-users), with no identified impacts, risks, or opportunities upstream/own operations for this topic.
- Materiality and strategy: Protection of sensitive customer information is material to Swedbank’s business model and strategy. Trust in how personal data is handled is critical. Products and services are designed to meet GDPR requirements, with structured policies, guidelines, and processes to ensure correct, secure data handling.
- Risk management: Swedbank maintains processes to identify, manage, and mitigate risks in personal data processing, including those arising from new or changed products, processes, and organizational changes. Poor data handling could cause privacy breaches, loss of trust, customer anxiety, and financial risk.
- Stakeholders affected: Existing and prospective customers, employees (including consultants) and their related parties, and visitors to branches. Vulnerable groups identified include minors, the elderly, and individuals with disabilities; customers with health-related insurance are at particular risk due to special-category data.
- Governance and policies (S4-1): Key documents include the Code of Conduct, Policy for Human Rights (aligned with the UN Guiding Principles and due diligence), Policy for Conduct Risk (product governance, data processing, market conduct), and Customer Complaint Policy (handling and prevention of complaints). Personal data rights are embedded within Swedbank’s human rights commitments and EU GDPR guidance.
- GDPR compliance: Swedbank is responsible for processing personal data only with a legal basis and with careful consideration of individuals’ rights, applying to all data subjects, not just customers. The bank provides detailed information to consumers and end-users about how their personal data is processed.
- Overall commitment: Robust personal data protection for all individuals to maintain trust, with impacts, risks, and opportunities for this topic identified as material.

structure.title: Strategy and business model, SBM-3
structure.heading: 6.2.2 Strategy and business model, SBM-3
structure.start_phrase: For Swedbank, the protection of sensitive customer information is imperative and customers must feel confident about how the Group handles personal data.
structure.summary:
- Focus and scope: Section S4 covers Swedbank’s information-related impacts on consumers and end-users across the value chain, identified as material in the Group’s assessment.
- Strategic importance: Protecting sensitive customer information is core to the business model and strategy. The bank designs products and services to meet GDPR requirements and operates structured policies, guidelines and processes to ensure correct, secure data handling.
- Risk management: Swedbank has processes to identify, manage and mitigate risks in personal data processing, including for new or changed products, processes and organizational changes, ensuring alignment with strategy.
- Potential impacts: Inadequate data handling can breach privacy, erode trust, create anxiety among customers, and pose financial risk to the bank.
- Affected stakeholders and vulnerable groups: Existing/prospective customers, employees and consultants (and related parties), and branch visitors may be affected. Higher-risk groups include minors, the elderly, individuals with disabilities, and customers with health-related insurance due to the sensitivity of health data.
- Governance and policies (S4-1): 
  - Code of Conduct (commitments on data protection and fundamental rights)
  - Policy for Human Rights (UN Guiding Principles; due diligence to prevent and address adverse impacts in own operations and business relationships)
  - Policy for Conduct Risk (principles for product design, distribution, data processing, and market conduct)
  - Customer Complaint Policy (standards for handling complaints and preventing recurrence)
- GDPR compliance: Personal data processing requires a legal basis and careful balancing of Swedbank’s interests with individuals’ rights; protections apply to all data subjects whose data Swedbank processes, not only customers. The bank provides detailed information to end-users about how their data is processed.
- Overarching commitment: Robust personal data protection is essential to maintain customer confidence and trust.

structure.title: Policies, S4-1
structure.heading: 6.2.3 Policies, S4-1
structure.start_phrase: Swedbank has policies and governance documents addressing impacts, risks and opportunities related to consumers and end-users, including handling sensi - tive customer information.
structure.summary:
- Scope and focus: Section S4 “Consumers and end-users” of Swedbank’s Annual and Sustainability Report 2024 covers information-related impacts on consumers/end-users, primarily in the downstream part of the value chain. It links to the Group’s materiality process (IRO-1) and maps impacts, risks, and opportunities for this topic.

- Materiality and strategic importance: Protection of sensitive customer information is deemed material and fundamental to Swedbank’s strategy. Extensive processing of personal data is inherent in financial services; improper handling can cause privacy breaches, loss of trust, customer anxiety, and financial risk for the bank.

- Governance framework: The topic is managed through key policies and governance documents:
  - Code of Conduct (commitments on data protection and fundamental rights)
  - Policy for Human Rights (UN Guiding Principles; due diligence across operations and relationships)
  - Policy for Conduct Risk (principles for product design, distribution, data processing, and market conduct)
  - Customer Complaint Policy (procedures to receive, resolve, and learn from complaints)
  Personal data rights are embedded within the bank’s human rights commitment and EU GDPR framework.

- GDPR-based management approach: Swedbank applies structured methods, policies, guidelines, and processes aligned with GDPR:
  - “Privacy by design” for products and services; legal basis required for all processing
  - Balancing the bank’s interests with individuals’ rights; applies to anyone whose data is processed, not just customers
  - Transparency through detailed information to end-users about data processing
  - Processes to identify, manage, and mitigate risks, including for new or changed products, processes, and organizational changes

- Stakeholders and vulnerable groups: Affected stakeholders include existing/prospective customers, employees and consultants (and related parties), and branch visitors. Higher-risk groups identified include minors, elderly people, individuals with disabilities, and customers with health-related insurance due to special-category data.

- Commitment and outcomes: Swedbank emphasizes robust personal data protection to maintain and strengthen trust, recognizing both potential negative impacts and opportunities in managing consumer information responsibly.

nodes.title: Protection of personal data in accordance with GDPR
nodes.heading: 6.2.3.1 Protection of personal data in accordance with GDPR
nodes.start_phrase: GDPR is based on established and internationally recognised conventions and principles for the protection of human rights.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and materiality: The S4 Consumers and end-users section covers Swedbank’s information-related impacts on consumers/end-users, identified as a material topic in the downstream value chain. Protecting sensitive customer data is central to the Group’s strategy. Mishandling data can cause privacy breaches, loss of trust, anxiety, and financial risk. Affected stakeholders include customers, prospects, employees/consultants, and visitors. Vulnerable groups include minors, the elderly, people with disabilities, and customers with health-related insurance.

- Governance and policies: Swedbank manages these impacts via the Code of Conduct, Human Rights Policy (aligned with UNGPs), Conduct Risk Policy, and Customer Complaint Policy. The right to personal data protection is treated as a human right. GDPR compliance underpins product/service design and data processing. Risk management follows the three lines of defence with independent controls, supported by a Data Protection Officer function. The Group does not currently track cases of failures to respect international principles in the downstream value chain.

- GDPR compliance and stakeholder information: Personal data processing requires a legal basis, with transparent information provided through websites, apps, branches, and customer meetings. Redress/compensation for data breaches follows GDPR and applicable law. The approach is aligned with SDGs, ILO, OECD, and UN guidance to promote ethical practices and human rights.

- Procedures for contact and rights (S4-2): Swedbank explains what data is collected, why, legal grounds, and processing practices, enabling customers to exercise their rights. Data handling adheres to GDPR principles: lawfulness/fairness/transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity/confidentiality, and accountability.

- Complaints and incident handling: Customer complaints are logged, reviewed quarterly, and used to drive improvements; cases close when repeat complaints cease. Employees receive regular information security training. In the event of non-compliance or incidents, affected individuals are notified without undue delay via direct channels or public notices if necessary. The CEO has ultimate responsibility; operational incident management lies with designated coordinators; effectiveness is tested via first- and second-line controls and benchmarking against authority guidance and case law. Customer satisfaction is monitored via regular surveys (NKI).

- Remediation (S4-3): Data Breach Guidelines govern incident response and evaluation of remedial sufficiency. Customers can escalate issues through the customer centre, branches, Data Protection Officer, complaints officer, customer ombudsman, and then to external authorities (e.g., ARN, IMY) or consumer advisory bodies.

- Data processors: A three-step due diligence process covers pre-contract assessments (technical/organizational/contractual measures), ongoing monitoring of security posture, and off-boarding to ensure return/erasure of personal data per contract.

- Actions and strategies (S4-4): Ongoing work spans regulatory compliance, risk identification, customer communication, and tool/system support. “Data protection by design and by default” is embedded in product and service development. Expected outcomes are not specified due to uncertainty; no progress metrics are provided as this is the first year of CSRD-aligned reporting.

- Training and awareness: Annual and role-based information security training is mandatory across all countries. Swedbank runs a yearly security month, regular briefings, and continuous phishing simulations. Mandatory and voluntary GDPR/data protection training aims to strengthen employee awareness and, indirectly, customer and societal understanding of personal data protection.

structure.title: Procedures for contacts, S4-2
structure.heading: 6.2.4 Procedures for contacts, S4-2
structure.start_phrase: Swedbank publishes information on external websites, at customer meetings and in applications about how and why the Group collects and processes cus - tomers’ personal information and data, and how customers can assert their rights.

- Human Rights Policy aligned with UN SDGs, UN Guiding Principles, ILO and OECD guidelines, emphasizing privacy and data protection; no current tracking of downstream human-rights noncompliance cases.
- Governance and risk management via three lines of defence with independent controls; CEO holds ultimate accountability for personal data handling; designated incident coordinators manage operations.
- Transparent customer information on data collection, purposes, legal bases, processing and retention, with access to DPO, customer service, and authorities; tools such as register extract forms provided.
- Seven GDPR-aligned data protection principles guide all processing: lawfulness/transparency, purpose limitation, data minimization, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity/confidentiality, and accountability.
- Complaint handling integrates customer feedback into improvements: complaints logged, reviewed quarterly, followed by evaluation, testing, and closure; actions routed through data breach or complaint processes as needed.
- Incident response and notification: affected individuals contacted promptly (phone/email/website); processes assessed through first- and second-line controls and by referencing regulatory guidance and case law; customer satisfaction tracked via surveys (NKI).
- Remediation (S4-3): Data Breach Guidelines define actions for incidents with significant negative impacts and require evaluation of action sufficiency; overall GDPR compliance embedded in policies and directives.
- Communication and escalation options: customers can elevate matters to the DPO, complaints officer, or customer ombudsman; if unresolved, external bodies (ARN, IMY, municipal advisers, Consumer Banking and Finance Agency) are available.
- Data processor governance through a three-step due diligence lifecycle: pre-contract assessment of safeguards, ongoing monitoring of security, and off-boarding with return/erasure of data per contract.
- Actions and strategies (S4-4): focus on regulatory compliance, risk identification, and customer communication; “data protection by design and by default” for products/services; no outcome metrics yet due to first-year CSRD reporting.
- Training: annual and role-based information security education, yearly security month, regular briefings, and continuous phishing simulations; mandatory and optional GDPR training to enhance employee and broader societal awareness.

structure.title: Procedures for remediation, S4-3
structure.heading: 6.2.5 Procedures for remediation, S4-3
structure.start_phrase: Swedbank complies with the GDPR and thereby the requirements set for handling personal data incidents.
structure.summary:
- Focus on Swedbank’s data protection and privacy practices, grounded in GDPR and broader human rights commitments (UN SDGs, UN Guiding Principles, ILO, OECD), emphasizing the right to privacy, family life, and protection of personal data.
- Governance and risk management: three lines of defence model with independent controls; CEO holds ultimate responsibility for lawful personal data handling, with operational duties delegated to incident coordinators and decision-makers; ongoing operational controls and regulatory/case-law benchmarking to identify and close gaps.
- Customer information and rights: clear, accessible disclosures across websites, apps, and customer meetings on what data is collected, legal bases, purposes, processing, retention, and contacts (including DPO); tools like register extract forms provided.
- Core data protection principles: adherence to seven GDPR-aligned principles (lawfulness/transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage minimisation, integrity/confidentiality, accountability).
- Complaints and feedback: centralized complaint registration, quarterly review and analysis, improvement cycle with testing and closure when issues cease; multiple contact channels (chat, phone, letters, branches); NKI surveys monitor customer satisfaction.
- Incident response and remediation: Data Breach Guidelines define actions for incidents with potential negative impacts; prompt notification to affected individuals via phone/email or public channels if direct contact isn’t possible; compensation/redress handled per GDPR and applicable laws.
- Escalation paths: if dissatisfied after internal review, customers can escalate to the DPO, complaints officer, customer ombudsman, and ultimately external bodies such as ARN, IMY, municipal consumer advisers, and the Swedish Consumer Banking and Finance Agency.
- Data processors: structured three-step due diligence—pre-contract assessment of technical/organizational measures, ongoing security monitoring, and off-boarding ensuring return/erasure of personal data per contract.
- “Privacy by design and by default”: embedded in product and service development; ongoing compliance supported by policies, instructions, and system tools.
- Training and awareness: mandatory annual and role-based information security training, annual security month, ongoing security briefings, simulated phishing; mandatory and optional GDPR/data protection training to raise employee and broader societal awareness.
- Limitations and disclosures: Swedbank does not currently track incidents of non-compliance with international human rights principles in the downstream value chain and does not measure customer awareness of its data protection work; no quantitative progress reporting yet as this is the first year aligning with CSRD; outcomes of future actions are not forecast due to uncertainties.

structure.title: Actions and strategies, S4-4
structure.heading: 6.2.6 Actions and strategies, S4-4

structure.summary:

nodes.title: Training
nodes.heading: 6.2.6.1 Training

- Data Protection Officer: accessible to all data subjects; oversees GDPR compliance, runs impact assessments and balancing tests, and reports quarterly/annually to the Board. Personal data retention aligns with purpose and legal obligations (e.g., AML, accounting); incidents are reported to authorities when required. No serious human rights incidents related to customers were reported during the year.

structure.title: Metrics and targets, S4-5
structure.heading: 6.2.7 Metrics and targets, S4-5
structure.start_phrase: Swedbank seeks to minimise the number and consequences of personal data incidents.
structure.summary:
- Follow-up and monitoring of data protection: Ongoing checks to ensure employees complete personal data handling training; a global system tracks EU regulatory changes and feeds an improvement process tied to customer complaints; incidents and improvements are handled via established personal data incident or complaint processes. Information on personal data handling is reviewed annually, and data protection controls are embedded when new systems/processes are developed. Individuals harmed by deficient procedures may receive compensation per law and internal rules.

- Data Protection Officer (DPO) and risk processes: Swedbank uses impact assessments, balancing of interests, and product processes to ensure processing is appropriate, necessary, fair, and proportionate, with mitigations documented. The DPO within Group Compliance monitors GDPR compliance and reports quarterly and annually to the Board against external requirements and the bank’s risk appetite. Customers, employees, and other data subjects can contact the DPO.

- Data processing principles and incident reporting: Personal data processing balances individual rights with the bank’s need to process data; retention follows purpose necessity and legal requirements (e.g., accounting, AML, capital adequacy, legal) and can exceed contract duration. Personal data incidents are reported to authorities when GDPR requires. No serious human rights issues/incidents related to customers were reported during the year.

- Customer ombudsman and complaints handling: A dedicated unit (seven ombudsmen, two complaint analysts) manages complaints and improvements, adhering to Swedish FSA timelines—aim to resolve within 14 days or inform the customer within 14 days if more time is needed.

- Metrics and targets for data protection: Objective is to minimize the number and impact of personal data incidents; methods are continually improved, but no outcome-based targets or time comparisons are reported. Group Compliance defines minimum standards and oversees compliance. Metrics cover:
  - Enquiries and complaints to the DPO: Significant increase in 2024 in enquiries (128) and complaints (112) from individuals; enquiries from data protection authorities decreased in 2024 (3). Data comes from data subjects and authorities; metrics are group-wide and not externally validated.
  - Information security training: High completion rates, though lower in Sweden and Latvia in 2024 (Sweden 93.9%, Estonia 99.0%, Latvia 97.3%, Lithuania 99.1%). Measured via internal training platforms; not externally validated.

- Business conduct (G1) scope: Covers whistleblower protection, supplier relationship and payment practices, corporate culture, and anti-corruption/bribery, with impacts/risks mapped across the value chain.

- Policies and governance for business conduct: Trust and a sustainable vision guide operations. Key governance documents include the Code of Conduct and policies on Conduct Risk, Conflicts of Interest, Financial Crime Risk, Personal Account Dealing, Enterprise Risk Management, and Operational Risk. Documents are available internally (public ones on the website). The Board and Group Executive Committee actively oversee culture; values permeate governance.

- Code of Conduct and culture controls: Applies to all employees/subsidiaries; included in onboarding. Annual ethics training and attestation are mandatory and tracked as KPIs. Regular employee surveys (three times yearly) support open culture and managerial follow-up. Mandatory role-based trainings are specified; ethics training addresses anti-corruption, bribery, and benefits, with guidance for real situations. Certain roles require licenses (e.g., SwedSec), with annual ethics components.

- Handling deviations, fraud, and violations: Employees are encouraged to report cultural or rule deviations. A risk-based anti-fraud framework includes preventive/detective controls and standardized processes for investigating regulatory breaches and internal fraud. High-risk processes have enhanced controls. Reports can be made to managers or the Internal Fraud unit; specialized units (Internal Fraud and HR/FM) investigate. Serious breaches can lead to employment actions (warnings, termination) based on investigation outcomes.

structure.title: G1 Business conduct

- Strategic context and oversight: Trust and ethical conduct underpin Swedbank’s purpose and vision of a financially sound and sustainable society. Corporate-culture issues are regularly addressed by the Board of Directors and the Group Executive Committee (including the CEO). References are provided to sections on strategy, culture, and governance.
- Policies and governance documents: Business conduct is governed by a suite of policies and standards available internally (and selected documents publicly), including the Code of Conduct, Policy for Conduct Risk, Policy on Conflicts of Interest, Policy on Financial Crime Risk, Policy on Personal Account Dealing, Policy on Enterprise Risk Management, and Policy for Operational Risk. These set cultural expectations and processes for managing business ethics.
- Code of Conduct and culture: The Code is the Group’s ethics policy, applicable to all employees and subsidiaries. It guides handling of business transactions and relationships and requires adherence to values, laws, regulations, and internal rules. Quarterly employee surveys gauge strategic alignment, leadership, and culture, with mandatory managerial follow-up.

Annual ethics training covers anti-corruption/bribery, assessment of benefits, and scenario-based guidance. - Detection, reporting, and response to misconduct: Employees are encouraged to identify and report incidents that breach rules or conflict with culture and values. Swedbank maintains a risk-based anti-fraud framework with controls to detect, prevent, and report suspected fraud, and a uniform process for investigating regulatory breaches and internal fraud.
- Reporting channels and controls: Technical and manual controls are deployed in high-risk processes. Deviations can be reported to line managers (who document and handle cases) or directly to the Internal Fraud unit. System support exists for identifying, reporting, and following up on internal risks and irregularities.

- Purchasing and supplier governance: Purchasing Instruction mandates transparency, honesty, competitiveness, and Code of Conduct compliance; Supplier Code of Conduct required (or equivalent policies), with deviations escalated to a sustainability committee; ~200 additional suppliers committed in 2024; continuous monitoring.
- Market surveillance: detection and reporting of suspicious transactions/orders under the EU Market Abuse Regulation to enhance market integrity.
- Whistleblower framework: EU Directive and Swedish law–aligned protections; multiple internal/external channels including anonymous, encrypted web portal run by an external provider; independent, authorized units manage cases, with conflict-of-interest safeguards; Board receives quarterly updates; 158 reports in 2024 (vs 126 in 2023); ongoing awareness and annual governance document updates; specialized mandate strengthens retaliation protection and process integrity.
- Culture and training: mandatory annual ethics training for employees and consultants (95% completion in 2024; revised with real-world dilemmas; bank confidentiality training planned); employees attest to the Code of Conduct; results reported to the Board from Q4 2024.
- Supplier relations (G1-2): digitized, risk-based procurement including conflict-of-interest checks, dual approvals, consultant background checks, and outsourcing risk assessments; staff training and guidance; sustainability questionnaires with >100 follow-up dialogues in 2024; action plans for underperforming suppliers; potential sustainability audits; material breaches can terminate contracts.
- Supplier program enhancements: Supplier Code update planned for Q1 2025 (ESG data, gift rules, whistleblower link); digitized identification of high-impact suppliers; building a central unit to assess first-line and strategic suppliers; no special procedures for vulnerable suppliers; compliance metrics track process adherence.
- Anti-corruption program (G1-3): policies (Code of Conduct, Financial Crime Risk Policy, Anti-Bribery & Corruption Instruction); guidance on gifts/events; in-depth mandatory training for high-risk contract owners; secondary occupation registration; supplier anti-bribery clauses and due diligence; independent investigations (Internal Fraud, HR&FM) with quarterly reporting to CEO/Board.

nodes.title: Supplier Code of Conduct
nodes.heading: 7.1.2.2 Supplier Code of Conduct

nodes.summary:
- Procurement governance and due diligence:
  - Checks for conflicts of interest, and supplier due diligence on corruption and bribery.
  - Duality in contract approvals to enhance objectivity and reduce corruption risk.
  - Background checks for consultants (criminal record, external commitments, financial status).
  - Outsourcing and critical supplier risk assessments covering information security, business continuity, and other areas.
  - Support tools: procurement training for employees and relevant stakeholders, guides/manuals, and sustainability-linked performance incentives.

- Supplier sustainability management:
  - Sustainability assessments via questionnaire covering environmental, social, and business ethics; follow-ups and activity plans where expectations are not met.
  - Over 100 supplier dialogues in 2024 to challenge and follow up on sustainability work.
  - Limited follow-up on local/certified suppliers due to perceived low need.

- Supplier Code of Conduct (SCoC):
  - Requirements on human rights, working conditions, business ethics, and environment; expected to cascade in the supplier value chain.
  - Recommends supplier whistleblower programs.
  - Non-signing triggers dialogue, escalation to the purchasing unit’s sustainability committee, and potential process deviation; violations constitute material breach and may end the relationship.

- Key actions and organizational enhancements:
  - Planned SCoC update in Q1 2025 to strengthen ESG requirements, gifts policy, and whistleblowing links across key geographies.
  - Digitalized identification of suppliers with significant sustainability impacts.
  - Expanded and centralized first-line supplier assessment capacity, including a central unit for strategic supplier management; intended to cover the full supplier base and support governance targets through 2026.
  - First year of CSRD-aligned reporting; no prior action progress metrics presented.
  - No special procedures for vulnerable suppliers.

- Monitoring and evaluation:
  - Procurement process compliance metric includes mandatory risk minimization pre-contract.
  - SCoC compliance verified via supplier follow-up questions.
  - Sustainability audits performed for major sustainability risks.
  - No distinct OPEX/CAPEX earmarked for sustainability action plans; costs embedded in ongoing operations.

- Anti-corruption and anti-bribery (G1-3):
  - Employee awareness through Code of Conduct training, new training on third-party risks, and guidelines on gifts/events.
  - Key governance documents: Code of Conduct, Policy on Financial Crime Risk, Instruction on Anti-Bribery and Corruption; accessible internally and publicly where applicable; Code translated in home markets.
  - Annual 30-minute ethics training (covers corruption/bribery basics, regulations, risk assessments), plus online training for employees/consultants on regulatory topics, benefits, and reporting; in-depth mandatory course for high-risk contract owners.
  - Employees register secondary occupations; suppliers must sign sustainability requirements or include equivalent anti-bribery clauses; targeted bribery/corruption questionnaires during procurement.
  - Allegations investigated by Internal Fraud and Group HR & Facility Management, independent from implicated units; Group Compliance assesses and reports outcomes to the CEO and Board quarterly.
  - Whistleblower channels for internal and external stakeholders to report suspected corruption and bribery.

nodes.title: Key actions
nodes.heading: 7.1.3.1 Key actions
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank took a number of key actions in its own operations during the year to address the risk of Swedbank being exposed to corruption and bribery.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: Anti-corruption, bribery prevention, and business ethics, with governance, training, monitoring, incident handling, and payment practices.

- Key actions taken:
  - Ethics training for all employees; targeted anti-bribery/corruption training for contract owners with high-risk contracts.
  - Annual updates of governance documents on bribery and corruption; introduction of Group-wide registers for events and sponsorships.
  - Ongoing monitoring of training completion rates; quarterly reporting on developments to the Board.
  - Group-wide corruption/bribery risk assessment to be completed in Q1 2025 with a final report to the Group Executive Committee.
  - Planned roll-out of Group-wide gifts and events training for managers and customer-facing staff.
  - No separate significant operating or capital expenditures identified for sustainability action plans; costs are embedded in normal operations.

- Metrics and oversight:
  - Aim: high business ethics and good conduct in financial markets.
  - Internal processes exist to monitor corporate culture, whistleblower protection, and anti-corruption, but Swedbank does not publish measurable outcome-oriented goals or time-series comparisons.
  - Group Compliance independently monitors compliance risks, evaluates internal rules and actions, sets minimum standards, and advises operations to align with the Board’s low risk appetite and zero-tolerance stance on bribery and corruption.
  - Regular risk assessments performed; the Chief Compliance Officer reports quarterly to the CEO and Board on effectiveness against risk appetite and regulations.
  - Supplier relationship management is monitored internally; if supplier risk exceeds appetite, it is escalated to the CEO and Board. No public outcome-oriented goals are disclosed.

- Incidents and investigations (G1-4):
  - Internal investigations are conducted for suspected rule breaches, including bribery/corruption; may lead to employment actions and police reports.
  - Operational risks identified are reported per risk procedures; HR & Facility Management and Group Compliance conduct quarterly follow-ups on suspected cases.
  - No 2024 data on employee convictions/fines for bribery/corruption due to lack of systematic follow-up; Internal Fraud unit will develop tracking for outcomes of police reports.
  - Metrics are not externally validated.

- Market surveillance under MAR:
  - STORs (notifications of suspected market abuse) monitored Group-wide and reported by country; not externally validated.
  - STOR counts: 2024: 121; 2023: 202; 2022: 57. Country breakdown in 2024: Sweden 44, Estonia 17, Latvia 55, Lithuania 5.
  - Prior increase linked to certain Baltic government agencies’ focus on specific trading patterns.

- Payment practices (G1-6):
  - Standard supplier payment terms: 30 days; average actual payment term ~31 days.
  - Average actual payment time: 27 days overall; 21 days for SMEs (suppliers with <250 employees, classified using Moody’s data).
  - Share paid within 30-day standard: 57% overall; 71% for SMEs. Share paid within current contractual terms: 71% overall; 58% for SMEs.
  - Operational approach: Baltics pay immediately after approval; Sweden pays on due date.
  - Metrics derived from internal invoice system covering ~90% of supplier invoices (Sweden and Baltic subsidiaries); not externally validated.
  - Legal proceedings relating to late payments are tracked; figure provided for SMEs, with separate overall status referenced.

nodes.title: Metrics and targets
nodes.heading: 7.1.3.2 Metrics and targets
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank seeks to achieve a high level of business ethics and good conduct in the financial market.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on anti-corruption and bribery controls: group-wide ethics training for all employees, targeted training for contract owners on high-risk contracts, annual updates to governance documents, and new registers for events and sponsorships. A Group-wide bribery/corruption risk assessment will be completed in Q1 2025, with expanded training for managers and customer-facing staff to follow. Progress is reported quarterly to the Board. Sustainability-related action plan costs are embedded in operating expenses, not separately identified.

- Governance, metrics, and oversight: Swedbank aims for high business ethics with zero tolerance for bribery and corruption and a Board-set low risk appetite. Group Compliance monitors compliance risks, evaluates rule effectiveness, proposes minimum standards, and advises operations; the Chief Compliance Officer reports quarterly to the CEO and Board. Internal processes track culture, whistleblower protection, anti-corruption, and supplier relationship management, but no public, outcome-oriented targets or time-series comparisons are published. Exceedances of supplier risk appetite are escalated to the CEO and Board.

- Incident handling and data gaps: Internal investigations address suspected rule breaches; employment actions may follow, and suspected crimes are reported to police. Operational risks identified are escalated per risk procedures. Quarterly follow-up of suspected corruption cases is conducted by HR & Facility Management and Group Compliance. Swedbank lacks 2024 data on employee convictions/fines for bribery/corruption due to no systematic follow-up; the Internal Fraud unit will build follow-up processes. Metrics are not externally validated.

- Market Abuse Regulation (MAR) surveillance: Group-wide systems support STOR (Suspicious Transaction and Order Report) monitoring and reporting by geography; data use is internal and not externally validated. 2024 saw 121 STORs (Sweden 44, Estonia 17, Latvia 55, Lithuania 5), compared to 2023: 202 and 2022: 57; the 2023 increase is linked to certain Baltic agencies’ focus on specific trading patterns.

- Supplier payment practices (G1-6): Standard supplier payment terms are 30 days; average actual payment terms are 31 days. Overall, Swedbank pays invoices in 27 days on average (21 days for SMEs). Payments within the 30-day standard: 57% overall, 71% for SMEs. Payments within agreed actual terms: 71% overall, 58% for SMEs. In the Baltics, invoices are paid immediately after approval; in Sweden, on the due date. SME status is determined via Moody’s (<250 employees). Metrics are based on internal invoice data covering ~90% of supplier invoices (including Baltic subsidiaries) and are not externally validated. Ten legal proceedings for late payments are outstanding for SMEs; none for all enterprises.

structure.title: Financial crime
structure.heading: 7.2 Financial crime
structure.start_phrase: The Financial Crime chapter concerns Swedbank’s reporting related to the Group’s work to combat financial crime.
structure.summary:
- Scope and definition: The chapter outlines Swedbank’s approach to combating financial crime, defined as money laundering, terrorist financing, bribery and corruption, facilitation of tax evasion, and fraud. Cybersecurity is covered elsewhere.
- Value chain and materiality: It maps where financial crime impacts and risks occur across the value chain and explains that, based on a double materiality assessment (including stakeholder input and lessons from past AML shortcomings), financial crime is a material, entity-specific topic for Swedbank.
- Risk and impact: Deficiencies in prevention and controls can harm customers and society, erode trust, and lead to financial penalties and sanctions.
- Governance framework: Swedbank uses a comprehensive set of Board-approved policies, CEO Instructions, and Group directives/guidelines to set risk appetite, responsibilities, controls, and reporting across financial crime risk categories. Public and internal documents are referenced.
- Core policies:
  - Policy on Financial Crime Risk sets overarching principles for AML/CFT, sanctions, anti-corruption/bribery, and facilitation of tax evasion.
  - Three CEO Instructions cover AML/CFT, financial sanctions, and anti-corruption, supported by directives that define internal controls and compliance measures.
- Fraud management:
  - Governed by the Policy on Enterprise Risk Management and the Policy for Operational Risk.
  - Instructions on Anti-Fraud Governance require a robust, risk-based framework to detect, prevent, and report fraud against the bank and its customers.
  - External Fraud Directive standardizes governance, processes, and preventive measures against external fraud.
  - Internal Fraud Directive standardizes investigations of regulatory breaches and suspected employee fraud.
- Cross-references: Links to detailed sections on corruption incidents and prevention (G1-3, G1-4), cybersecurity (G3, 3.4), materiality processes (IRO-1), governance documents (MDR-P), and risk note (3.7).

- Risks and impacts: Deficiencies in controls can harm customers and society, erode trust, and expose the bank to fines and sanctions; references to further risk details provided in the risk note.
- Governance framework: Describes a layered set of Board‑approved policies, CEO instructions, and Group directives that set risk appetite, roles and responsibilities, controls, and reporting for financial crime prevention. Governance documents are available internally and selected ones publicly.
- Core policies: Policy on Financial Crime Risk sets overarching principles; supplemented by CEO instructions on AML/CFT, financial sanctions, and anti‑corruption, plus directives specifying internal controls and compliance measures for AML/CFT and sanctions.
- Fraud management: Governed by the Enterprise Risk Management Policy and Operational Risk Policy, with Instructions on Anti‑Fraud Governance requiring a risk‑based prevention framework. External Fraud Directive standardizes management and prevention of external fraud; Internal Fraud Directive sets a uniform process for investigating employee breaches and suspected internal fraud.
- Reporting references: Bribery and corruption prevention and incidents are reported in dedicated sections (G1‑3, G1‑4); cyber security is covered in a separate note; additional policy references and governance document listings are provided.

nodes.title: Money laundering, financial sanctions, corruption and facilitation of tax evasion
nodes.heading: 7.2.2.2.1 Money laundering, financial sanctions, corruption and facilitation of tax evasion
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank has adopted a Policy on Financial Crime Risk, which sets out the over - arching principles for Swedbank’s financial crime prevention work, such as money laundering, financing of terrorism, breach or circumvention of financial sanctions, bribery and corruption, and the facilitation of tax evasion.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and definition: The chapter covers Swedbank’s work to combat financial crime, defined as money laundering, terrorist financing, bribery and corruption, facilitation of tax evasion, and fraud. Bribery/corruption metrics are reported under G1-3/G1-4, and cyber security is covered separately (note G3, section 3.4).
- Value chain mapping: Identifies where impacts, risks and opportunities related to financial crime occur across the value chain (upstream, own operations, downstream), with references to the broader IRO process for materiality.
- Materiality and risk: A double materiality assessment, informed by internal experts, stakeholder input, and historical shortcomings, concludes financial crime is a material, entity-specific topic for Swedbank. Deficiencies in AML/CFT and fraud controls can harm customers and society, erode trust, and create financial risks via fines and sanctions. Further detail is in risk note section 3.7.
- Governance framework: Swedbank’s Board-approved policies, CEO Instructions, and Group directives/guidelines establish risk appetite, roles, controls, and reporting, aiming to minimize negative impacts and prevent the bank from being exploited. Public and internal governance documents are referenced (MDR-P).
- Policies on financial crime: A Group Policy on Financial Crime Risk sets overarching principles for AML/CFT, financial sanctions, anti-corruption, and facilitation of tax evasion, supplemented by three CEO Instructions (AML/CFT, financial sanctions, anti-corruption) and related Group directives detailing required internal controls and compliance measures.
- Fraud management: Fraud prevention and investigations are governed by the Policy on Enterprise Risk Management and Policy for Operational Risk, plus Instructions on Anti-Fraud Governance mandating a robust, risk-based framework. nodes.title: Fraud
nodes.heading: 7.2.2.2.2 Fraud
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank’s fraud prevention work and investigation of fraud cases is governed by the Policy on Enterprise Risk Management and the Policy for Operational Risk.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and definition: The chapter covers Swedbank’s work to prevent financial crime, defined as money laundering, terrorism financing, bribery and corruption, and facilitation of tax evasion; fraud is also addressed. Bribery/corruption performance is reported under G1-3 and G1-4, and cyber security is covered separately (note G3, section 3.4). A value chain view indicates where impacts, risks, and opportunities occur upstream, in own operations, and downstream.

- Materiality and context: Given Swedbank’s central role in payments, financing, investments, and advice, the bank is exposed to financial crime risks. A double materiality assessment—drawing on internal experts, stakeholder input, analyses/surveys, and lessons from historical AML shortcomings—concluded financial crime is a material, entity-specific topic. Deficiencies in controls can harm customers and society and create financial risks via loss of trust, fines, and sanctions. Further detail is referenced in risk note section 3.7.

- Governance framework: Swedbank relies on Board-approved policies, CEO Instructions, and Group directives/guidelines to set standards, responsibilities, and risk appetite for financial crime risk management. Governance documents are available internally (and some publicly) and are catalogued under Swedbank governance documents (MDR-P).

- Policies on ML/TF, sanctions, corruption, and tax evasion facilitation: A Group-wide Policy on Financial Crime Risk sets overarching principles across these areas. It is supplemented by three CEO Instructions (AML/CFT, financial sanctions, anti-corruption) and by Group directives that define required internal controls and measures for AML/CFT and sanctions compliance.

- Fraud governance: Fraud prevention and investigations are governed by the Policy on Enterprise Risk Management and the Policy for Operational Risk, plus Instructions on Anti-Fraud Governance mandating a robust, risk-based framework and controls to detect, prevent, and report suspected fraud affecting the bank or its customers. An External Fraud Directive ensures a consistent group-wide approach and preventive measures for external fraud, while an Internal Fraud Directive standardizes investigations of employee regulatory breaches and suspected internal fraud (with further details in Policies, G1-1).

nodes.title: Actions and preventive measures
nodes.heading: 7.2.3 Actions and preventive measures
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank works actively to identify and prevent all forms of financial crime where Swedbank is used for illegal transactions using the proceeds from criminal activity or for transfers intended to finance terrorism.
nodes.summary:
- Focus and scope: Swedbank’s actions and preventive measures against financial crime, including money laundering, terrorist financing, sanctions breaches, bribery and corruption, and facilitation of tax evasion, as well as its fraud prevention strategy, governance, and performance trends.

- Core financial crime controls:
  - Risk-based framework grounded in a robust, data-driven risk assessment.
  - Customer due diligence, customer risk assessment, ongoing transaction monitoring, sanctions screening, and regulatory reporting of suspicious activity.
  - Strong compliance culture supported by tailored training programs for all employees based on role- and risk-specific needs.
  - Continued investment in technology to enhance screening and monitoring, with heightened focus on sanctions compliance given geopolitical developments (e.g., Russia’s war against Ukraine).

- Collaboration and information sharing:
  - Active participation in SAMLIT Financial Crime Prevention with Swedish police and major banks.
  - Multiple information-sharing initiatives with law enforcement and industry peers to improve understanding, detection, and prevention.

- Fraud strategy and initiatives:
  - Three-pillar approach: prevent, detect, investigate.
  - Ongoing enhancements to product/channel security, transaction monitoring, and processes.
  - Implementation of the Swedish Bankers’ Association’s cross-industry anti-fraud package (targeted for full implementation by end of 2025).
  - Dedicated Anti-Fraud Programme to reduce customer losses and coordinate efforts across units.
  - Support for affected customers, including stopping fraud in progress, fund recovery, and handling complaints per established procedures.
  - Interbank fraud collaboration to share trends, modus operandi, best practices, and assess the impact of new measures.

- Governance, metrics, and risk appetite:
  - Low risk appetite for financial crime set through internal regulations and monitored by Group Compliance.
  - Officer for controlling and reporting obligations (OCR) within Group Compliance reports quarterly and annually to the Board on AML/CTF effectiveness and alignment with risk appetite.
  - Internal regulations define prohibited activities, high-risk scenarios requiring enhanced measures, and explicit controls for risk owners.
  - Annual, data-driven general risk assessment across customers, products, geographies, and channels; continuous monitoring via a data application.
  - Swedbank does not publish outcome-based external KPIs for these areas but conducts internal follow-up to evaluate effectiveness.

- Recent trends and outcomes (H1 2024):
  - Overall fraud volume and customer losses decreased versus the prior year, mirroring national statistics.
  - Significant decline in vishing/smishing; rise in investment fraud; other fraud types largely stable.
  - Improvements attributed to strengthened controls, product/process security, and higher societal awareness.

nodes.title: Money laundering, financial sanctions, corruption and facilitation of tax evasion
nodes.heading: 7.2.3.1 Money laundering, financial sanctions, corruption and facilitation of tax evasion
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank works actively to identify and prevent all forms of financial crime where Swedbank is used for illegal transactions using the proceeds from criminal activity or for transfers intended to finance terrorism.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines Swedbank’s comprehensive approach to preventing financial crime and fraud.

- Scope and commitment: Addresses money laundering, terrorist financing, financial sanctions violations or circumventions, bribery and corruption, and facilitation of tax evasion. Emphasizes regulatory, systemic, and moral obligations, including actions within Swedbank and downstream in the value chain.
- Risk-based framework: Enterprise-wide identification and assessment of financial crime risks driving controls. Core components include customer due diligence and risk assessment, transaction monitoring, suspicious activity reporting, and sanctions screening of customers and transactions.
- Training and culture: Strong focus on compliance culture supported by mandatory training for all employees and tailored, risk-based programs for higher-risk roles and areas.
- Technology enablement: Ongoing investment in tools and systems to enhance sanctions screening and monitoring, strengthened in response to geopolitical developments, particularly Russia’s war against Ukraine.
- Collaboration: Active participation with Swedish law enforcement and other banks, including SAMLIT Financial Crime Prevention and multiple information-sharing initiatives to improve understanding and operational effectiveness.
- Fraud strategy: Three-tier approach—prevent, detect, investigate—backed by enhanced product and channel security, reinforced transaction monitoring, and streamlined processes. A dedicated Anti-Fraud Programme coordinates efforts, targets reduced customer losses, and ensures implementation of the Swedish Bankers’ Association’s industry-wide measures (aimed for full implementation by end-2025). Support for affected customers includes stopping ongoing fraud, recovering funds, and established complaint handling for unauthorized transactions.
- Industry coordination on fraud: Joint initiatives among major Swedish banks, the Swedish Bankers’ Association, and SAMLIT to share fraud trends, modus operandi, and assess the impact of implemented measures.
- Governance, metrics, and risk appetite: Low risk appetite for financial crime formalized through internal regulations. While Swedbank does not publish measurable outcome metrics, effectiveness is followed up internally. Group Compliance independently monitors regulatory compliance risks; the AML Officer for Controlling and Reporting (OCR) within Group Compliance reports to the Board quarterly and annually. Internal rules define prohibited activities, higher-risk circumstances requiring enhanced measures, and explicit control responsibilities for risk owners.
- Data-driven risk assessment: Annual, comprehensive assessments across customers, products, geographies, and channels, with applications that allow risk owners to continuously monitor alignment with risk appetite.
- 2024 fraud trends: Overall fraud remained high but declined in H1 2024 versus the prior year; customer losses also decreased, attributed to stronger controls, processes, and greater public awareness. Notable decline in vishing/smishing; increase in investment fraud; other fraud types largely stable.

nodes.title: Fraud
nodes.heading: 7.2.3.2 Fraud
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank’s work to prevent and investigate fraud is based on three strategic levels of action: prevent, detect and investigate.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Swedbank’s actions and preventive measures against money laundering, terrorist financing, sanctions violations, bribery/corruption, and facilitation of tax evasion, plus its fraud prevention approach, governance, and observed trends.
- Risk-based framework: Robust group-wide risk assessment drives controls; continuous process, routine, and control development for CDD, customer risk assessment, transaction monitoring, sanctions screening, and regulatory reporting.
- People and culture: Strong compliance culture supported by mandatory and role-specific, risk-tailored training to strengthen high-risk areas.
- Technology: Ongoing investments in systems that enhance screening and monitoring; heightened focus on sanctions compliance due to geopolitical developments, notably Russia’s war against Ukraine.
- External collaboration: Active participation in SAMLIT and other information-sharing initiatives with law enforcement and major banks to improve understanding, detection, and prevention of financial crime.
- Fraud strategy: Three-pronged approach—prevent, detect, investigate—supported by stronger product/channel security and enhanced monitoring; alignment with the Swedish Bankers’ Association’s industry-wide measures targeted for full implementation by end-2025.
- Anti-Fraud Programme: Bank-wide coordination to reduce customer losses, implement industry measures, and improve incident handling; direct customer support to stop ongoing fraud, recover funds, and manage claims.
- Governance, metrics, and oversight: Low risk appetite for financial crime; internal follow-up without publishing outcome-based targets; Group Compliance independently monitors regulatory compliance; OCR function within Group Compliance reports quarterly/annually to the Board on AML/CFT performance.
- Internal regulations: Define prohibited activities, higher-risk circumstances, required enhanced measures, and explicit controls for risk owners to maintain comprehensive oversight.
- Annual, data-driven risk assessment: Evaluates exposure by customer, product, geography, and channels; tools enable risk owners to monitor alignment with risk appetite in detail.
- 2024 trends: Overall fraud volumes and customer losses decreased in H1 2024; notable decline in vishing/smishing; rise in investment fraud; other fraud types largely stable.

nodes.title: Metrics and targets
nodes.heading: 7.2.4 Metrics and targets
nodes.start_phrase: Swedbank has a low risk appetite for financial crime.
nodes.summary:
- Focus and scope: Swedbank’s actions to prevent financial crime, including money laundering, terrorism financing, violations/circumventions of financial sanctions, bribery and corruption, and facilitation of tax evasion.
- Risk-based framework: A robust, data-driven enterprise-wide risk assessment informs customer due diligence, customer risk scoring, transaction monitoring, suspicious activity reporting, and sanctions screening.
- Continuous improvement: Ongoing development of internal processes, routines, and controls; emphasis on combining strong compliance culture with mandatory baseline and role-specific training.
- Technology enablement: Investments in advanced screening and monitoring solutions, especially for sanctions compliance, heightened by geopolitical developments (e.g., Russia’s war against Ukraine).
- Collaboration and information sharing: Active participation in SAMLIT (with police and Sweden’s largest banks) and other initiatives; interbank fraud collaboration via the Swedish Bankers’ Association to share trends and modus operandi.
- Fraud strategy: Three-tier approach—prevent, detect, investigate—supported by stronger product/channel security, enhanced transaction monitoring, and streamlined processes. A dedicated Anti-Fraud Programme coordinates efforts, targets reduced customer losses, and implements the industry-wide package of measures slated for full rollout by end-2025.
- Customer support: Ongoing assistance to stop active fraud, recover funds, restore accounts, and guide victims to report to police and submit unauthorized transaction claims.
- Governance, metrics, and risk appetite: Low risk appetite formalized through internal regulations; Group Compliance (including the AML Officer for Controlling and Reporting, OCR) independently monitors and reports quarterly/annually to the CEO and Board. Internal rules define prohibited activities, higher-risk scenarios, and required controls. Annual, data-driven general risk assessment covers customers, products, geographies, and channels; thresholds tied to risk appetite trigger escalations; progress in fraud prevention reported to top management.
- Outcomes and trends: Overall fraud volumes and customer losses decreased in H1 2024 versus 2023, notably for vishing/smishing; investment fraud increased; other fraud types remained stable.

structure.title: Disclosure requirements in ESRS standards covered by the Sustainability Report, IRO 2
structure.heading: 8 Disclosure requirements in ESRS standards covered by the Sustainability Report, IRO 2
structure.start_phrase: The table below is a list of the disclosure requirements included in Swedbank’s Sustainability Report 2024.
structure.summary:
- Purpose and scope: A comprehensive index (IRO‑2) showing which ESRS disclosure requirements Swedbank covers in its 2024 Sustainability Report, where each appears (page references), and how they link to the bank’s materiality process (IRO‑1). It also maps required datapoints from related EU legislation (SFDR, CRR/Pillar 3, EU Benchmark Regulation, EU Climate Law) and flags where items are included, not material, not applicable, or subject to phase‑in.
- General information and governance: Disclosures on the basis of preparation, specific circumstances, strategy/business model/value chain (SBM‑1/2/3), stakeholder interests (including S1 and S4 perspectives), processes to identify and assess material impacts, risks and opportunities (IRO‑1), governance roles (GOV‑1/2), integration of sustainability in incentives (GOV‑3), due diligence statement (GOV‑4), and internal controls over sustainability reporting (GOV‑5).
- Environmental (E1 focus): Transition plan for climate change mitigation, climate‑related policies, actions/resources, targets, and metrics; reporting of Scope 1, 2, 3 and total GHG emissions and intensity; alignment with MDR policy/action/target/metric minimums; several energy and physical risk datapoints noted as not material, not applicable, or phased in.
- Social:
  - S1 (own workforce): Policies, engagement, remediation channels, actions and effectiveness, targets, and a wide set of metrics (diversity, adequate wages, training/skills, health and safety, work‑life balance, remuneration/pay gap), with MDR linkages.
  - S4 (consumers and end‑users): Policies, engagement, remediation, actions and effectiveness, targets, and metrics.
  - Selected S1/S2/S3 datapoints on human rights, child/forced labour risks, accidents, and grievance mechanisms included; many value chain and incident‑type datapoints marked not material or phase‑in.
- Governance (G1): Business conduct and culture, supplier relationship management, anti‑corruption and anti‑bribery prevention/detection, incidents, payment practices; related policies, actions, targets and metrics; references to whistleblower protection and fines.
- Company‑specific: Financial crime prevention presented under MDR policy/action/target/metric structure.
- Cross‑regulatory mapping: A detailed table links ESRS datapoints to SFDR Annexes, Pillar 3/Article 449a templates, Benchmark Regulation (Paris‑aligned/Climate Transition Benchmarks), and EU Climate Law, indicating where Swedbank reports each item, and explicitly noting:
  - Not applicable areas (e.g., involvement in controversial weapons, certain fossil fuel/chemical/tobacco activities; several E1 physical risk portfolio metrics under phase‑in).
  - Not material topics (e.g., several pollution, water/marine, biodiversity/ecosystem, and waste datapoints; some human rights incident indicators; GHG removals/carbon credits).
  - Phase‑in items for physical risk exposures and some safety metrics.
- Navigation aid: Page references throughout the tables enable direct location of each disclosure within the Annual and Sustainability Report 2024 (Board of Directors’ report section).

structure.title: Tables according to the EU Taxonomy regulation
structure.heading: 9 Tables according to the EU Taxonomy regulation
structure.start_phrase: The EU Taxonomy-specific tables for credit institutions are tables 0 to 5 below.
structure.summary:
- Purpose and scope: EU Taxonomy-specific disclosure for a credit institution (Swedbank) presented as Tables 0–5, prepared under the EU Taxonomy Regulation. References to further information on pages 78 and 98–99.
- Table 0 (Summary of KPIs 2024):
  - Total environmentally sustainable assets (based on counterparty Turnover KPI): SEK 64,290m; corresponding Green Asset Ratio (GAR) stock: 3.37%. A CapEx-based view is also provided (3.59%).
  - Additional KPI: GAR flow 2024 shows SEK 10,264m; ratio indication c. 3.08% (3.15% CapEx-based).
  - KPI coverage over total assets: 73.39% for stock; 99.63% for flow.
  - Exclusions: 34.79% of assets excluded from the GAR numerator and 26.61% from the denominator for stock; 53.97% excluded from numerator and 0.37% from denominator for flow.
  - Trading book, financial guarantees, and assets under management (AUM) KPIs indicated; note that fees and commissions income and trading book KPIs will first be published in the 2025 annual report.
  - Footnote: all environmentally sustainable assets based on CapEx KPI total SEK 68,504m.
- Table set on assets for GAR calculation (Turnover-based):
  - 2024 detailed breakdown by environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO).
  - For each objective, exposures are shown as taxonomy-eligible and taxonomy-aligned, with flags for Use of Proceeds (UoP), transitional, and enabling activities.
  - Counterparty and product categories: financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, investment firms, management companies, insurance undertakings), non-financial undertakings, households (including loans collateralised by residential property, building renovation loans, motor vehicle loans), local government financing, and collateral obtained.
  - 2024 highlights include significant taxonomy-aligned household exposures tied to residential mortgages (SEK 58,221m) and aligned exposures to non-financial undertakings; CE/PPC/BIO show smaller aligned volumes focused on non-financial undertakings.
  - Assets excluded from GAR numerator but included in denominator: SMEs and other NFCs not subject to NFRD/CSRD, non-EU counterparties not subject to NFRD/CSRD, derivatives, on-demand interbank loans, cash and cash-equivalents, and other assets (e.g., goodwill).
  - Assets not covered by GAR: central governments and supranational issuers, central bank exposures, and trading book exposures.
  - Totals are provided for GAR-covered assets, assets excluded from numerator/denominator, assets not covered for GAR, and total assets.
- Off-balance sheet exposures:
  - 2024: financial guarantees and AUM disclosed with taxonomy-eligible and taxonomy-aligned amounts, including instrument splits (debt and equity).
  - Footnote clarifies totals for guarantees and AUM refer to overall volumes, not only holdings in NFRD/CSRD companies.
- 2023 comparatives (Turnover-based):
  - Same structure for CCM/CCA/WTR with taxonomy-eligible and -aligned views; CE/PPC/BIO largely not populated for 2023.
  - Household aligned mortgage exposures (SEK 23,257m) and non-financial undertaking aligned amounts are shown.
  - Exclusions, not-covered assets, totals, and off-balance sheet (financial guarantees and AUM with debt/equity splits) are presented for 2023 to enable year-on-year comparison.

nodes.title: Assets for calculation of GAR

A footnote clarifies totals cover overall volumes, not only holdings in NFRD/CSRD companies.

nodes.title: GAR sector information
nodes.heading: 2. GAR sector information
nodes.start_phrase: Turnover based
nodes.summary:
- Source and scope: Extract from Swedbank’s Annual and Sustainability Report 2024 (Board of Directors’ report), section “2. GAR sector information,” presenting EU Taxonomy-aligned Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures for 2024.
- Framework and structure:
  - Breakdown by NACE sector codes.
  - Split by client type: Non‑financial corporates subject to NFRD vs. SMEs/other non‑financial corporates not subject to NFRD.
  - Two performance metrics: turnover-based and capex-based.
  - Coverage of all six environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO).
  - For each sector and objective: Gross carrying amount (SEKm) and “of which environmentally sustainable.”
- Turnover-based highlights:
  - Comprehensive sector-by-sector tables for CCM/CCA/WTR and for CE/PPC/BIO, with totals.
  - Aggregate total shows SEKm 38,981 gross carrying amount and SEKm 5,774 environmentally sustainable.
  - Significant taxonomy-aligned turnover appears in:
    - Production of electricity (NACE 35.11) with a large CCM-aligned share.
    - Renting and operating of own or leased real estate (68.20), notably CCM and CCA-aligned amounts.
    - Manufacture of railway locomotives and rolling stock (30.20), and selected machinery/equipment categories (e.g., lifting/handling equipment, non‑domestic cooling and ventilation).
    - Pipeline transport (49.50) showing full alignment in the disclosed amount.
    - Waste collection (38.11) contributing under CE/PPC.
  - Many sectors show zero or minimal alignment for CCA and WTR; electricity transmission (35.12) shows zero alignment.
- Capex-based highlights:
  - Parallel sector-by-sector disclosure for CCM/CCA/WTR and CE/PPC/BIO, with totals.
  - Aggregate total shows SEKm 38,981 gross carrying amount and SEKm 9,985 environmentally sustainable, indicating higher capex alignment than turnover alignment.
  - Largest capex alignment in:
    - Production of electricity (35.11) with substantial CCM-aligned capex.
    - Real estate activities (68.20) across CCM and CCA.
    - Selected manufacturing of equipment and transport (e.g., instruments and appliances, cooling/ventilation equipment, railway rolling stock, medical and dental instruments).
    - Waste collection (38.11) under CCM and contributions under CE/PPC.
  - Several activities (e.g., electricity transmission 35.12) remain at zero aligned capex.
- Overall observations:
  - Climate Change Mitigation dominates the environmentally sustainable amounts; Adaptation, Water, and the four non‑climate objectives (CE, PPC, BIO) are smaller and concentrated in a few sectors.
  - Alignment is largely concentrated in NFRD‑subject non‑financial corporates; SMEs/other corporates often show limited or zero aligned amounts.
  - Detailed, auditable mapping of exposures to EU Taxonomy via NACE codes supports transparency of Swedbank’s green financing footprint by sector and objective.

nodes.title: GAR KPI stock

Breakdowns include “of which” categories for use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities. Figures are reported for assets included in both the numerator and denominator.
- Portfolio breakdown: Disaggregates by asset type and counterparty category—loans and advances, debt securities (including use-of-proceeds bonds), equity instruments; financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, management companies, insurance undertakings), non‑financial undertakings, households (mortgages, building renovation loans, motor vehicle loans), and certain local government exposures.
- 2024 turnover-based highlights:
  - Total taxonomy-eligible ≈ 55.71% of covered assets; taxonomy-aligned ≈ 3.37%.
  - Alignment is largely driven by the household mortgage portfolio (households: eligible 54.47%, aligned 3.05%).
  - Non-financial undertakings: eligible ≈ 0.96%, aligned ≈ 0.30; financial undertakings: eligible ≈ 0.28%, aligned ≈ 0.02.
  - Minimal exposure to CE/PPC/BIO objectives (eligible roughly 0.12/0.02/0.01; aligned near 0.00–0.01).
  - “Of which” amounts for use-of-proceeds and transitional/enabling activities are very small; coverage of total assets in denominator ≈ 73.39%.

  - Households still dominate aligned share (3.05%); non-financial undertakings aligned ≈ 0.52%.

- 2023 turnover-based highlights:

  - Households aligned ≈ 1.24%; non-financial undertakings eligible ≈ 0.61%, aligned ≈ 0.12.
  - Use-of-proceeds and transitional/enabling negligible; total assets coverage ≈ 74.42%.
  - Tables for CE/PPC/BIO are largely blank/immaterial for 2023.
- 2023 capex-based highlights:
  - Total taxonomy-eligible ≈ 55.89%; taxonomy-aligned ≈ 1.41%.

  - Total assets coverage ≈ 74.42%.
- Overall message: The GAR is predominantly driven by the mortgage book; taxonomy alignment increases from 2023 to 2024 in both turnover- and capex-based views, while exposures to other environmental objectives beyond climate remain very limited, and use-of-proceeds/transitional/enabling shares are minor.
